Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an iterative procedure for discovering such a representation, with an analysis of its properties leading to a parameterized algorithm solving the issue in time proportional to the number of nodes to the power of 4.5, improving upon the existing time complexity of proportional to the number of nodes to the power of 6 in an earlier solution. The approach has further implications for resolving the circle completion problem and detects isolated clusters in an unstructured environment. The methodology involves a style-specific representation suitable for two-dimensional visualizations. The paper provides a concise summary of the style, its representation, and the approach to enhance it, before illustrating the application of the style to a set of linear representations that can be easily parsed. The paper's results have been validated through comprehensive experiments conducted using a wide range of realistic datasets, with a particular emphasis on datasets comprising variable-sized clusters. The findings have been compared against an existing state-of-the-art solution, bi-directional branch-and-cut, on both small and large-scale datasets, revealing the superiority of the new approach, the level of performance exceeding the level achieved by bi-directional branch-and-cut by a significant margin. The paper concludes by analyzing the approach's potential limitations, presenting some promising research ideas, and offering a brief overview of the related work. The paper style has been made available for public use through an associated repository. The paper has been published in the proceedings of the 2023 ACM Conference on Human Information Interaction Technology. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking with a Redundant Trunk Truster Robot (RTTR) using a hybrid controller. In contrast to traditional bipedal robots, RTTRs have multiple degrees of freedom that could potentially be used for walking, and our task-specific approach takes advantage of these freedoms to enhance stability and mobility. Our controller combines two separate strategies to guide the trunk's movement: a passive approach that leverages the natural dynamics of the robot, and an active approach that directly influences the trunk's motion using thrust. To validate our method, we will compare the performance of RTTR with only passive trunk movement. Our results show that using a hybrid controller leads to improved stability, as measured by the orientation of the trunk, and reduces the energy expended per step by approximately 10%. Additionally, we found that our approach allows for efficient recovery from unexpected disturbances, including those that affect balance and traction. To demonstrate the practical applications of our approach, we conducted experiments using a non-slip surface and found that the hybrid controller enables the robot to maintain its balance in challenging situations. Our findings also highlight the importance of properly configuring the controller to maximize the benefits of thrust-supported locomotion. In the course of this research, we encountered several difficulties, including determining the optimal degree of freedom for the trunk, calculating the moment arm of the thrust, and developing a method to characterize the hybrid controller. We hope that our solutions to these problems will be useful to other researchers working with similar robot designs. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/RTTR-Group/. The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Key Research and Development Project of Guangdong Province, and the Science and Technology Planning Project of Guangdong Province. The findings were published in a conference paper titled "Thruster-Assisted Bipedal Locomotion Using a Redundant Trunk Robot" at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation in 2020, and in a journal article titled "Thruster-Assisted Bipedal Locomotion Using a Redundant Trunk Robot" in the Journal of Intelligent Robotics Systems in 2021. The current version of the robot weighs approximately 45 kilograms and is designed to move at a speed of one meter per second. In order to make efficient use of power-consuming CPU frequency options, this work presents the HyperDegrade framework. Designed to work with dynamic voltage and frequency scaling technologies, HyperDegrade determines the optimal highest CPU frequency that should be employed by each process on a multi-processor system based on multiple factors, including task characteristics, hardware limitations, and performance objectives. The proposed method takes into account ProcArray's processing capabilities, memory access patterns, data transfer rates, and temperature effects, among other factors, to provide a precise solution to the problem of determining the ideal CPU frequency for each process. Alternatively, a more efficient dynamic solution is also provided for real-time applications. The development of HyperDegrade includes a case study involving an x86 processor and an ASIC processor, as well as experimental evaluations using industry-standard benchmarks and performance optimization tools. The results show that HyperDegrade's static and dynamic solutions are capable of reducing average system frequency by 37% and 20% while still meeting performance and energy efficiency requirements, and that the framework is compatible with existing IP cores with only minimal modifications, reducing the average frequency degradation to 12%. The research also highlights an important phenomenon called the "degrade effect" where reducing frequency among some processes can lead to an increase in frequency for other processes, allowing for an average system frequency increase of 6% with no additional performance or energy efficiency costs. The proposed framework and associated findings are suitable for a wide range of processors, not just the x86 processor, and can be applied to various processing scenarios, from inter- to intra-processor environments, using a single processor with multiple cores. The development of HyperDegrade provides a comprehensive and industry-relevant example, the Intel Celeron J4125 processor, to help reduce frequency degradation and increase average system frequency to 37% with the static solution and 20% with the dynamic solution. Our analysis shows that combining two specific local moves yields a more powerful operation capable of untangling any classical or welded links. We further prove that combining three particular local moves results in an operation equivalent to combining two Chordia moves, thus providing a different approach to achieving combined move closure. Additionally, our research finds that combined local moves close the family of torus-knoted welded links, which was previously unclosed. Moreover, our analysis determines the minimal number of combined local moves required to untangle any welded link, and establishes a relationship between this number and the combined Chordia moves required for untanglement. We believe these findings represent important contributions to the study of combined move closure. We propose a new method for proving that a particular link can be untangled through a specific sequence of local moves, and we achieve combined move closure for the family of torus-knoted welded links by demonstrating such a sequence for any torus-knotted link. Our research also clarifies the distinction between the concepts of combined move closure and link polynorphism. We further show that combining two local moves results in an operation equivalent to linking polynomial equivalence, which provides a different approach to achieving linking polynomial closure. Additionally, our analysis finds the linking polynomial for the torus-knotted links, and we demonstrate that combining three local moves results in an operation equivalent to knot polynomial closure. We believe these findings represent important contributions to the study of linked objects in three-dimensional space. In complex tasks that involve simultaneous sub-tasks across different locations, a common goal is to synchronize tasks efficiently. This synchronization can be achieved by assigning tasks to locations based on their level of computation requirement, positioning them in a hierarchical manner. When the distribution of tasks varies significantly, traditional hierarchical approaches may not be effective. In this paper, a decision-making framework is developed for strategic synchronization across different locations, taking into consideration their specific computation capabilities and spatial distance, and prioritizing locations with a higher level of computation capability over those with a lower level. The paper also analyzes various performance scenarios to demonstrate the effectiveness of this conservative policy. Finally, an application to a swarm of robots is presented, where each robot represents a location with a particular computation capability at a specific spatial position, and they must synchronize their task of collecting and delivering packages. In this scenario, the policy is shown to promote a hierarchical structure among the robots. One possible criticism of this approach is that it may lead to locations with a lower computation capability being overwhelmed by an excessive amount of tasks, but this issue is addressed by introducing a threshold of desired computation capability that must be met before a location is considered suitable for task assignment. The approach is further tested on a regular two-dimensional grid of robots, where it is shown that it can efficiently distribute tasks evenly, compared to a random assignment. The developed policy can be implemented through a simple learning algorithm that enables robots to determine the desired level of computation capability for a specific location with sufficient precision. The paper also discusses various possible modifications to the policy, including introducing a delay between tasks or incorporating a memory component that retains information from previous time steps. One such modification involves adding a threshold of desired computation capability that must be met before a location is considered suitable for task assignment, which can be achieved by training a deep neural network to learn the distribution of task assignment from past data, and using this learned distribution to determine the desired level of computation capability for a specific location. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these modifications on the policy and possible future directions, such as incorporating uncertainty or noise into the computation capability of locations. The developed policy is validated through simulations conducted on regular and random grids of robots, where it is compared to a random assignment, and found to be more efficient in distributing tasks evenly. The paper also discusses the connection between the policy and optimal control theory, and presents a theoretical analysis of the policy's performance in an ideal scenario, which demonstrates its convergence to an equilibrium state. The paper concludes by summarizing the main findings, discussing the related work

This paper delves into the realm of federated learning, particularly in its vertical version, where entities collaborate to train a model across mutually exclusive data sets. Our focus shifts from ensuring model accuracy to exploring real-world privacy constraints in privacy-sensitive applications. We examine two common privacy mechanisms: secure averaging and federated learning with partial model sharing. However, we also investigate two possible attacks on these mechanisms: a new linear regression-based assault on users and a new machine learning-based assault on users, demonstrating the effectiveness of these attacks in exposing personal information from a trained model. We then outline a protocol for these attacks and provide specific examples, including one that compromises the privacy of a model trained for classification in a scenario involving gender determination. We also review general strategies of defending against such assaults, including boosting, smoothing, and differential privacy, and propose a novel approach, dubbed linear contrastive training, capable of enhancing privacy by constraining the model's output in the face of attacks. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $N$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $N$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $N$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves simple and broad generalization, demonstrating superior results on more challenging datasets such as the recently launched AFLW2019-3D. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghristian/SADRNet.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves identifying the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically using BERT, have led to significant gains in WSD accuracy by employing a zero-shot or few-shot learning approach.  However, these methods have limitations when applying to words with numerous senses, as they require access to pre-trained models with the target senses.  To address this challenge, we develop a novel framework called Context-gloss WSD, which leverages context-gloss pairs to enhance the context for better WSD performance.  We pair context with desired gloss definitions for target senses and use them to fine-tune BERT.  To mitigate data overhead, we adopt a strategy called definition sampling.  Our proposed context-gloss enhancement leads to significant gains in multiple evaluation metrics.  Interestingly, we observe that simply pairing context with gloss definitions without further fine-tuning also yields notable WSD performance.  To demonstrate the versatility of our approach, we apply it to both few-shot and zero-shot WSD benchmarks and notice a positive impact on their results.  We also explore other options for context-gloss pairs, such as using Wikipedia summaries, and discover they are effective in their own right.  Ultimately, our context-gloss WSD framework provides a versatile method that can be combined with existing approaches and other context-gloss sources, offering numerous possibilities for future research.  We make our code available at https://github.com/TextGroup/Context-gloss WSD.  We achieve zero-shot WSD results of 79.1% on SenseVal and 53.5% on Multilingual SenseVal and few-shot WSD results of 82.3% on SenseVal and 56.3% on Multilingual SenseVal.  We discover definition sampling is effective and that using Wikipedia summaries yields zero-shot WSD results of 78.5% on SenseVal and 52.3% on Multilingual SenseVal.  We believe these findings highlight the importance of specifying context quality and obtaining it may lead to better performance in other NLP tasks.  We propose three future research directions: (1) investigating the connection between context quality and other NLP tasks, (2) exploring other sources of high-quality context, and (3) developing methods to automatically create high-quality context. Named after Gibbs, Cramer, and Sanov, three prominent mathematicians, the large deviation principles in question concern the behavior of normalized sums of negatively log-probabilities associated with sequences of correlated letters. These principles enable an expansion of associated functional forms, yielding a quadratic guarantee valid for extremely large-sized collections of sequences. The underlying model, which can be represented as an irreversible Markov process, results in sequences being highly correlated and asymmetric. The study demonstrates that the large deviation principles in question hold true for not only Markov models but also more broad, abstract settings based on ergodic measures. The development of associated generating functions, along with the large deviation principle for weighted sums of empirical measures, also play crucial roles in achieving this goal. The research presented here builds directly upon previous works by Cramer, Sanov, and Gibbs, with the most related results sharing structural similarities to the underlying model used in Dirichlet large deviation principles. The second section focuses on developing the weighted empirical measure, along with the associated generating functions. The third and final section delves into the specific examples of random independent and identically distributed matrices generated from the Dirichlet distribution. This kind of surface is not subject to boundary constraints and typically has unique properties that distinguish it from constant mean curvature surfaces. Our primary goal is to explore the structure of these surfaces, referred to as minimal surfaces within a homotopy class, and demonstrate the existence of a minimizing surface that can be obtained through a gradual process of relaxation, guided by the mean curvature flow. We also establish criteria for the uniqueness of these surfaces, primarily in the context of hyperbolic geometry. Moreover, we derive explicit formulas for the area of these surfaces, including in the context of hyperbolic geometry. The use of mean curvature flow allows us to animate the process of surface relaxation, which may be visualized for certain types of surfaces in the hyperbolic geometry. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. This pattern of shapes existing together together is particularly notable because it occurs at low spins, and is driven by a strong monopole interaction, counter to previous understanding that it only occurs at high spins, and is dominated by the quadrupole interaction. This discovery in 64Ni marks the third instance of shape coexistence with 0+ and 2+ states, following 44Cr and 70Zn, and sheds new light on the monopole interaction's role in nuclear physics. The detailed analysis of its effects has been made publicly available through the Monte Carlo shell model code, and will aid in studying other nuclei where shape coexistence with 0+ and 2+ states is anticipated. The dominant configurations contributing to the 64Ni states have been identified, and the results suggest that the delopped s-d shell monopole interaction is responsible for grouping the 0+ and 2+ states together, although further studies are needed to confirm this interpretation. The extensive data set and analytical code have been made available for the scientific community to study 62Ni, which is thought to have a simple 0+ ground state state, but may also exhibit shape coexistence similar to 64Ni. The research was conducted by an international team of scientists, involving the Bocksburg Array at iThemba LABS in South Africa, the Large Acceptance Spectrometer at University of Jyvaskyla in Finland, the TPC at University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom, and the RIKEN Radioacive Beam Factory in Japan, using a 64Ni beam created by fragmentation of 64Ni, 64Cu, and 64Fe, and targeting 64Ni, 62Ni, and 60Ni nuclei. The Monte Carlo shell model code used for the analysis can be obtained from the Monte Carlo Shell Model for Medium-Mass Nuclei website. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The resulting models prove significantly more resilient to data partitioning, enable tighter upper and lower bounds, and significantly reduce the risk of overestimating performance. The outcome is a simpler yet more effective performance estimation method that reduces variance and bias and our empirical evaluation shows this approach yields models that are not only more accurate but also more readily transferable to novel, unseen data. The code for the project is publicly available at https://github.com/ghoul4936/jkfold. We investigated the effects of photon recoil in a system of overlapping absorption lines, using a single laser beam to interact with an ultracold sample of $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the overlap of the lines, we observed significant deviations from traditional lorentzian shapes, particularly in the center of the absorption lines. Our results demonstrated that the inclusion of Raman scattering, which results from the interaction of counter-propagating laser beams, is necessary to accurately explain the phenomena observed. Our analysis also revealed that the width of the absorption lines is influenced by the intensity of the laser beam, following a pattern consistent with the effects of Raman scattering. Nevertheless, we found that the interaction requires an extremely high saturation parameter, which must be taken into account in experiments involving linearly polarized light. Furthermore, we explored the phenomenon of effective line shape changes resulting from the interaction, and discovered that the width of the absorption lines is influenced by the velocity of the atoms, which could provide a novel approach to measuring atomic velocities in experiments. Our research was conducted using a setup that simultaneously allows for precise velocity control and measurement of velocity distributions through the absorption of a single laser beam, offering a novel application of single-beam absorption spectroscopy. Moreover, we discussed the relationship between Raman scattering and velocity changes, which results in velocity distribution changes over time, offering another perspective on the phenomenon. Finally, we discussed the relevance of our findings to real-world scenarios, citing examples such as atmospheric absorption spectra and astronomical signals, as well as satellite remote sensing, where the effects of Raman scattering could influence velocity distributions and, in turn, impact the accuracy of temperature and humidity measurements. Our results have been incorporated into a code available online, along with related discussion. The code demonstrates how to calculate the velocity distribution of a particle system following a linear absorption process, and provides a novel approach to measuring atomic velocities in experiments, offering a novel application of single-beam absorption spectroscopy. The code is compatible with MATLAB and can be downloaded from the webpage of the publication. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of fluids undergo shear thickening, a sudden and extreme increase in resistance that can cause fluids to turn solid-like. Despite its surprising nature, the causes and effects of shear thickening remain poorly understood, especially in highly concentrated mixtures that can represent real-world situations. In this study, we challenge a long-standing misconception that shear thickening only occurs in highly congested mixtures and take a more general approach by analyzing the relationship between shear stress and rate of change of stress. This simpler analysis reveals the specific stress at which shear thickening begins and ends, revealing that it follows a universal pattern that can be applied to various mixtures, including those that are concentrated or diluted. Furthermore, by examining the width of the shear thickening transition region, we gain insight into the conditions under which mixtures become completely solid-like. We validate our findings using a simple model that provides a clear physical explanation for these patterns, also known as power laws. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable precise methods forces practitioners to use large samples, which can consist of up to 10,000 permutations, to achieve the desired level of precision in their results. To address this challenge, we introduce an efficient algorithm that generates the paired-permutation test distribution quickly, reducing the number of necessary samples to just 100 permutations. To further increase the test's precision, we develop two methods to structure the test distribution. Theoretical and empirical results demonstrate that combining these two distribution-structuring methods leads to a highly precise result, roughly equivalent to using a 10,000-sample set, while significantly reducing computation time. Our proposed approach has been applied to real datasets and has shown impressive precision at a much lower cost compared to traditional methods. The code for this paper is available at GitHub.com/alexbiewald/precise-paired-permutation.

We define a new object called a "loom" to generalize the concept of a triangulation in metric spaces with angles. Looms can vary depending on the measure used, but their core structure remains consistent. This discovery enables us to create a specific type of triangulation called a "veering triangulation," which is characterized by its ability to remain invariant under changes in the measure used. Veering triangulations have a distinctive property where the same edge is repeatedly shared between adjacent triangles. This property can also be expressed as the absence of specific loop configurations. Our research reveals that the curvature of a veering triangulation is constantly decreasing over time and will eventually reach zero. In addition, we establish that veering triangulations are stable under small changes in the measure used and classify their points of instability. Furthermore, we define two types of looms, complex and simple looms, and demonstrate that simple looms are equivalent to veering triangulations. This representation highlights the loom's stability information and edge weights as geometric features in three-dimensional space. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Standard Model as the primary source of Higgs bosons and calculate double Higgs production cross sections at these colliders to establish a baseline. However, due to the sub-zeptobarn sensitivity of these detectors to the primary Standard Model process, this contribution can be negligible. We then explore the capacity of these colliders to detect double Higgs production resulting from BSM Higgs interactions, incorporating EFTs that describe light Higgs couplings and heavy BSM particles. In particular, we analyze the effectiveness of detecting Higgs pairs in the $b\bar{b} \tau^+\tau^-$ final state at 3 TeV energy, concluding that future electron-positron colliders with the desired sensitivity can detect this process with just one event per year with a heavy dipole operator of mass $\sim 400$ TeV. Furthermore, we examine the detectability of non-SM Higgs interactions through kinematic distributions of associated jet pairs, identifying $\phi\phi$, $\rho\rho$, and $A A$ production as promising signatures of BSM Higgs physics. In the context of EFTs, we analyze these processes as they result in heavy Higgs resonances that can be identified through colliders by searching for large Higgs pair masses, exceeding 1 TeV in some cases. In addition, we explore the effectiveness of combining data from different processes and final states, considering processes like $hhjj$ and $hhhh$, as well as combinations of and with other Standard Model processes, finding that this combines can significantly enhance the sensitivity to BSM Higgs interactions, with some combined processes yielding results that are over an order of magnitude more sensitive to certain BSM Higgs interactions than any individual process or final state. Finally, we provide a comprehensive listing of detectable BSM Higgs interactions at these colliders, offering actionable advice for future experimental and theoretical investigations. Our analysis applies to both the classical Einstein theory and its modifications, including $f(R)$ gravity. We demonstrate that the conserved current is directly linked to the variation of the action with respect to the Lagrangian density, bypassing the need for a Lagrangian density in some cases. We also examine the consequences for the conserved current in these scenarios. Furthermore, we discuss the relationship between Noether currents and conserved charges in covariant theories. Our analysis includes an examination of the specific case of $f(R)$ gravity. We conclude by investigating the applicability of the conserved current to the Einstein-Hilbert action in cases where the metric component is not differentiable. Our results also demonstrate that the conserved current can be expressed in an integral form that is independent of the metric component, allowing us to define the Lagrangian description in these cases. We investigated the drag experienced by a cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material saturated with fluid, and found that its direction is not necessarily aligned with its motion. By considering the stability of the object's interface with the surrounding fluid and the properties of the granular material, we derived an equation for its anisotropic component. In the case of low speeds, this anisotropy is particularly notable, and its extent can be influenced by the force required to maintain contact between the object and the bed. Additionally, our research revealed that the drag experienced by the object is directly proportional to the force maintaining its contact with the bed, and this proportionality holds true regardless of the object's speed or the properties of the surrounding bed. These conclusions were confirmed through numerical simulations of an object moving through a saturated granular bed. We also compared our theoretical findings to existing experimental data obtained by moving a cylindrical object through a layer of fluidized grains, and found that our model agrees with these results when the object's speed is high. However, when the object's speed is low, our model predicts drag anisotropy that is not reflected in the same way by these experimental data. Furthermore, our research highlighted the importance of considering the objects' speed, the properties of the granular material, and the objects' shape in drag anisotropy, which may reflect the complexities revealed by our data set. We also analyzed the stability of the interface between the object and the surrounding fluid, and found that drag anisotropy can occur even when this interface is stable. This situation is different from the findings of an earlier study, which only observed drag anisotropy when the interface was unstable. We were able to explain the differences between our results and those of the earlier study by analyzing the forces acting on the object and the properties of the bed, and we believe that our explanation has broader applications to other complex phenomena involving interacting components. Moreover, our research highlighted the link between drag anisotropy and the objects' speed, which can result in drag anisotropy even when the object's speed is high, although this situation is less common. We also found that rotating objects moving through a layer of fluidized grains always experience drag anisotropy, which can result in the formation of stable patterns of motion. These patterns are influenced by the objects' speed, the properties of the bed, and the objects' shape, and we were able to predict them through our model. Which has broader implications to other complex phenomena involving rotating components

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for triangular flow, by comparing it across different collision types and centralities. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on collision energy, our findings showed triangular flow to be unaffected by energy changes. However, our analysis discovered a notable relationship between the anisotropic geometry of collisions and resulting triangular flow, revealing that triangular flow tends to decrease as collisions become more central. This pattern held true for both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Additionally, our research demonstrated that triangular flow can be distinguished based on geometric properties, either through the use of eccentricity divided by initial density or through flow anisotropy divided by particle density, with each denominator varying across different collision centralities. Notably, we found these two representations to be interchangeable, as they describe identical physical properties. To further understand this behavior, our model simulated collisions at various angles, which revealed that the direction of the triangular anisotropy shifts depending on the position of collisions within the transverse plane. This information can be combined with results from the beam energy scan to provide a comprehensive understanding of triangular flow's properties. Moreover, our analysis demonstrated that the ratio of elliptical to triangular flow remains constant across different collision centralities, which may be utilized as a reference for future experiments. Lastly, our research highlighted potential pathways for investigating initial geometric conditions in detail, which is essential for gaining a deeper insight into triangular flow's behavior. All in all, our study's findings can be applied to a wide range of collisions, from the beam energy scan to those with higher energies, and can be utilized by future experiments to a large extent. This research was conducted in collaboration with X.Y. Li, C. Zhang, Z. A. Peng, and Y. G. Ma.

The ATLAS experiment has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This level of precision has been reached by maintaining high sensitivity to certain processes, such as rare $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays, which are calculated to occur very infrequently, and by achieving a high level of accuracy in measuring the CP-violating process $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. The most more recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration for these processes are as follows: the consistency of its measurements with the most recent theoretical predictions from the Standard Model of particle physics has been verified, and in particular, the likelihood of the smallest of these processes occurring very infrequently is found to be $1.36 \times 10^{-7}$, and this level of infrequency is now too great for the experiments at the CERN particle accelerator to detect on their own, but it can still be measured accurately by combining the data from the ATLAS and CMS detectors, which together yield a value of $1.17 \times 10^{-7} \pm 0.01 \times 10^{-7}$. Furthermore, the accuracy of the measurement for the smallest of these processes is expected to continue to improve as the amount of data available to the ATLAS and CMS detectors increases, and this level of precision is expected to be sufficient to detect a phenomenon that could potentially occur many times more frequently, which would indicate the presence of new physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. The measurement for the largest of these processes, which involves the decay of B mesons into the particles that make up the phi meson, has also been improved to the point where it is possible to measure the angle of a complex mathematical pattern that arises as a result of this decay, and this level of precision is expected to continue to improve as the amount of data available to the ATLAS and CMS detectors increases, and it is likely to yield valuable information about the properties of the Standard Model of particle physics, which could in turn indicate the presence of new physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. This study aims to bridge this gap by exploring implicit connections between Krylov methods and preservation-based discretizations, and demonstrating how preserving certain properties can be achieved through modification of the Krylov method itself. Specifically, we propose modifying the residual formulation to enforce preservation properties, and demonstrate that doing so results in the solution preserving both conservation and non-negativity. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce Adversarial Metric Learning for self-supervised scene flow estimation, leveraging metric learning and adversarial training to concentrate on precise flow estimation while ignoring less accurate solutions. This approach leads to a straightforward model that effectively estimates scene flow without additional supervised training. We assess our method on the presented benchmarks, demonstrating its capability to effectively estimate scene flow in various settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/yangyaohs/3DSceneFlow-Benchmark.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. We further explore the relationship between precision and speed, demonstrating ways to balance operational energy efficiency and classification precision. In one example, when operating at 1 MHz speed and using 4 neurons per layer, we achieved an accurate classification rate of 96.5% on a census database. We also examine the relationship between precise classification and data sampling techniques, presenting a novel adaptive sampling approach that addresses issues related to attribute imbalances and noisy data. In cases where data is abundant and comprehensive, such as image recognition, this approach may not significantly improve results; however, on other datasets, including the census example mentioned above, we observed a 7% to 10% improvement in accuracy compared to traditional training methods. We believe that this proposed RNN model has vast potential applications in various real-world scenarios. We have made our code available online at: https://github.com/yousef-abel/RNN.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call policy learning in containerized microservices. During operation, Timeloops enables autonomous system call policy learning by analyzing the behavior of individual services and combining their results. It utilizes a novel approach called Differential Policy Learning, which compares the system call requirements of a service at successive time intervals. This approach yields a differential policy indicating the changes in needed permissions. Differential policies are further integrated into a hierarchical policy framework. The efficacy of Timeloops is demonstrated through experimental data collected from benchmark applications including Redis, NGINX, and Apache Airflow. The results show that Timeloops achieves comparable efficiency with a manual approach while reducing the system call learning time by approximately 86%. Furthermore, the development of Timeloops showcases that system call learning is compatible with secure sandboxes, which use seccomp filters, by preventing the services from accessing the network during the learning process. This is illustrated through an experiment involving Timeloops and the benchmark application Apache Airflow. The findings have been made available on the website timeloops.github.io. The success of soccer teams can largely depend on high-stakes moments like penalty kicks, given the significant scoring difference with these situations. To improve performance in such critical phases, we propose a deep reinforcement learning approach to optimize players' shooting techniques. By leveraging a rich state space and a simple action system, our method enhances the strategic decision-making of shooting choices and technique execution. In order to accommodate limited training information, our algorithm incorporates a robust value function feature learning process and a shooting choice policy, resulting in the publication of our code on GitHub. Experimental applications on real tournament data demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, with shooting technique policies learned from both small and large datasets yielding a 15% and 5% increase in scoring average, respectively. Additionally, we discovered that the standard penalty kick technique is the most optimal for the majority of situations, despite the potential benefits of alternative methods. In contrast to traditional game simulation methods, our approach also provides concrete policy guidance to coaches and players. To further validate our method, shooting technique policies were learned from simulated game scenarios, resulting in outcomes indistinguishable from the actual tournaments. In the process of exploring different dataset scales, we encountered an interesting phenomenon related to the diversity of learned shooting choices and technique execution, which could be useful for coaches in identifying areas for improvement with their players. In the context of soccer, we also introduced a novel shooting choice challenge and a technique execution evaluation metric, which could be applied to real games, allowing for the quantitative assessment of the shooting techniques used by players in critical situations. We provide explicit examples of potential functions that satisfy certain conditions, which are necessary to ensure the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that combines the Klein-Gordon equation and anharmonic oscillator. By examining these conditions in context, we investigate the relationship between wave solution stability and properties of the potential function. Specifically, we analyze how the presence of singular points near the origin in the potential function's spectrum affects the stability of solitary waves. Furthermore, we compare the number of singular points and their multiplicity in the context of the anharmonic oscillator to determine conditions under which solutions are stable. Our study builds upon previous research by Bartshein and Galaktionov, who established the connection between the number of singular points and solution stability. We also offer a new proof of the necessity of non-degeneracy in the harmonic oscillator context. Additionally, we provide a correction to their results by removing the assumption of even symmetry in the potential function. Moreover, we examine the relationship between the number of singular points and solution stability in the anharmonic oscillator case and offer a new approach to guaranteeing solution stability through the introduction of a suitable modification to the potential function, such as adding a delta function supported at the origin. This allows us to ensure the existence of solutions with finite energy that contain oscillatory components in the context of the anharmonic oscillator. Our findings are relevant to the study of anharmonic Schrödinger equations, Klein-Gordon equations, and other related models. We offer a brief introduction to these models in the paper. Our approach involves using the anharmonic oscillator as a tool to understand the relationship between the number of singular points and solution stability, as well as providing a way to generate solutions with specified properties, such as the presence of boundary layers, through the introduction of a suitable modification to the potential function. We conclude by outlining a program of research that aims to explore the connection between the number of singular points and solution stability in the anharmonic oscillator case, as well as the anharmonic Schrödinger equation, with the goal of ensuring the presence of components in solutions with finite energy. We derive new conclusions regarding the rank and embedding depth of a quadratic extension of Q. Specifically, its rank is equivalent to 2, while its embedding depth is 2 if and only if its ring of integers is a Gruenwald ring, otherwise it is 3. Additionally, we establish that its ideal class group is isomorphic to a subgroup of the Galois group generated by the conjugation map. Furthermore, we show that, for a number field F, the rank of its ring of integers is less than half the class number if and only if it has no quadratic subfields. This implies that the rank of a quadratic extension is always greater than half the class number, as expected. Our results generalize and expand upon existing theorems of Leopoldt. Our approach to proving these results involves applying a recent theorem of Burdges to our specific context. Our analysis also includes an in-depth examination of an example involving the quadratic extension Q(\sqrt{19}) for comparison purposes. Our findings regarding the rank and embedding depth of a quadratic extension can be extended to certain cubic and higher-degree extensions, as we discuss in the final section of our paper. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) occurs. In this study, we use high-resolution imaging to examine the retinal neuroepithelium in developing zebrafish to determine the underlying characteristics of IKNM. We found that, in contrast to previous findings of periodic movement, fish with a normally developing retina exhibit random movement patterns on the retinal plate. We confirmed the diffusive nature of this movement by demonstrating that the distribution of a single retinal cell nucleus follows a diffusion model over a short period, and that the rate of migration is highest near the outer edge of the retina. We propose that cell nucleus migration serves a different purpose in this region, where it facilitates random layer formation rather than determining the specific position of future neural layers. We also reveal that abnormal movement patterns are observed in fish with retinal developmental anomalies, and that the distribution of nuclei in these cases deviates from a perfect ring shape due to altered IKNM patterns. We conclude that random movement of cell nuclei in the neuroepithelial tissue in the developing retina ensures proper layer formation through diffusion, and that this process may have broader implications for layer formation in other neuroepithelial tissues. The data collected during this study have been deposited in a publicly accessible repository for review by the scientific community. The findings presented in this study have been previously published in a different format in the BMC Biology journal. The current work differs from the previous publication in that it includes additional results, a more in-depth discussion of methods and analyses, and a commentary on the relationship between cell nucleus migration and layer formation. The current work also addresses potential concerns related to the previous publication, specifically that interkinetic nuclear movement may not be necessary for proper layer formation, and that random movement may result in uneven layer distribution. The findings presented in this study demonstrate that interkinetic nuclear movement is essential for even layer distribution, and that random movement is responsible for distributing nuclei evenly throughout the neuroepithelial tissue. Previous studies codified specific imaging scenarios, such as video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, into fixed code-based models. By recognizing that many imaging problems share a common underlying structure, specifically the presence of sparse signals and mixing matrices, we propose a more flexible approach using code-based models that can be tailored for a variety of applications. We demonstrate that codifying specific imaging scenarios directly into density models can lead to suboptimal performance compared to standard code-based models, and that our general code-based model can achieve superior performance in various imaging tasks. Furthermore, we provide a method for deriving specific density models from a general code-based model, enabling the codification of prior knowledge about particular imaging scenarios. Experimental results confirm the benefits of this proposed approach in various imaging scenarios. We also explore compressive video sensing and video density models in an emerging area of research. We've developed a precise field theory for polar active liquids in the presence of random obstacles in dimensions greater than 2. This theory incorporates incompatibility requirements and reveals the existence of a unique, non-zero order parameter in the composite system. This result demonstrates that the interaction between particles and the environment does not reduce the dimensionality of the system below its intrinsic spatial domain, even when spatial constraints become prevalent. This is shown to affect the spatial and temporal scaling properties of the system's dynamics. Specifically, as the fraction of the incompressible phase increases, the system's diffusion slows down while its rotational diffusion speeds up. Furthermore, we find that the system's behavior transitions from a highly disordered state to a more organized state as the fraction of the incompressible phase grows, and this growth accelerates with time. This is achieved through a detailed analysis of the system's dynamics using numerical methods, which validate our field theory predictions. These findings have been compared with existing simulations of the NPT DPD model. Quantum harmonic oscillators were historically integrated exactly using path integrals, showcasing a complex integral that is now understood with a varied set of methodologies. In this study, a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to time-dependent driving forces was analyzed using the perturbation theory, and by limiting the approach to first-order perturbation, the researchers achieved an integrally representable expression consisting of a fractional integral. A direct application of this representation facilitated numerical validation through Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. The results were verified against the exact solution, and also against the perturbation approach for both its original and expanded versions, demonstrating the validity of the method. The study of this model, especially with its time-dependent characteristics, allowed for an insightful comparison with experimental data obtained through junction spectroscopy in graphene systems, specifically for a particular defect found under an iron adsorption site. The research was concluded by highlighting the potential of the method for further investigation of more complex systems. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by causing a net torque that influences their spin periods and orientations. As the YORP effect leads to a steady increase in rotational velocity, it follows a linear pattern with time, thereby creating a triaxial shape that can be described by a set of Euler angles in a non-inertial reference frame. To determine the magnitude of this impact, researchers need to consider various factors including the solar flux, reflection properties, and geometric characteristics of the asteroids. To quantify these characteristics, the YORP time constant can be expressed as $\tau_{YOP} = \frac{3Q \Delta R^2 (1-\gamma)}{6\sqrt{15}\sigma T^2 r^2}$, where $Q$ is the efficiency of the Yarkovsky effect per unit of irradiation, $\Delta R$ is the diameter of the equatorial bulge, $\gamma$ is the average of the reflectivity coefficients for perpendicular and parallel light transmission, $\sigma$ is the average cross-sectional area of the asteroid, $r$ is the distance from the Sun to the asteroid, and $T$ is the rotation period of the asteroid. To calculate the YORP time constant for the asteroids 1992 SK, Toro, and Geographos, we need to determine the reflection properties and geometric characteristics of these objects. To achieve this, we used various techniques including the analysis of light curves, thermal infrared observations with the Spitzer space telescope, and high-resolution images from the Hubble space telescope. By comparing the predicted and observed values of the YORP time constant for these asteroids, we found that the reflection properties and geometric characteristics we determined were accurate, and also gained insight into their evolution over time, as well as the effects of missions and stellar perturbations on their rotation velocities. Additionally, we found that the YORP time constant for these asteroids is within the range of $10^4$ to $10^6$ years, and that their rotation velocities increased by more than $10^{-5}$ radians per year due to the YORP effect. Furthermore, we found that the reflection properties and geometric characteristics of these objects remained relatively stable over time, as evidenced by the similar values of the YORP time constant derived from light curves and high-resolution images, as well as the effects of missions and stellar perturbations on their rotation velocities. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests that the VTC's animacy structure is characterized by a gradient that reflects the distance between a central, entity-defining region, potentially related to the neural processing of abstract concepts. However, the extent to which integral aspects of entity representation, such as agency and intentional behavior, are accounted for within this framework is unknown. In the present study, a computational model was utilized to assess the relationship between the VTC's animacy structure and the expression of animacy in a visual scene, specifically focusing on the presence of living things, agency, and intentional behavior. The results revealed a distinct, cross-participant pattern of animacy representation associated with agency and intentional behavior in particular, which exhibited a distinct gradient than that described by the basic level/superordinate level structure. The findings presented in this study highlight the complex nature of the VTC's animacy organization and highlight the importance of considering the varied aspects of entity representation in the construction of the VTC's animacy structure. The methodological approach employed here is also introduced as the 'animacy scene decoding' technique, which is readily applicable to other cognitive contexts. The study's conclusions are further validated through the use of a novel, synthetic dataset generated utilizing generative adversarial networks. The implications of these findings for the ongoing debate regarding the VTC's animacy structure are discussed in detail, along with potential avenues for research into the complex mechanisms of the VTC's animacy structure and the context of movie processing, visual scene representation, and agency and intentional behavior. The code and generated datasets for this study are available online. The study's findings highlight the intricate relationship between the VTC's animacy structure and the expression of animacy in visual scenes, and as such, provides a framework for future research into the complex mechanisms underlying the VTC's animacy structure. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. The appendices include realistic simulation scenarios that mimic various real-life scenarios, such as an early super-spreader event during the COVID-19 outbreak in Wuhan, China, and a scenario explaining the rapid spread of the norovirus at a military barracks in the United Kingdom in 1962. The paper addresses the integration of vector magnetic field data with remote sensing observations in solar physics. It is demonstrated that, via the use of transverse magnetic field estimates from magnetohydrodynamic models, corrections can be made for bias in the measurement of the total magnetic energy density. However, such corrections are shown to introduce previously absent bias in the measurement of the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line of sight. A new correction method is therefore developed, taking into account both the characteristics of the measurement system and the use of transverse magnetic field estimates from MHD models. This approach is tested using synthetic data and observed data from the Sun, and it is found that it is effective in both cases. The results indicate that the new method is capable of recovering the original distribution of the transverse magnetic field component with a precision of 99.5%, while the precision of the measurement of the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line of sight is improved from 37% to 5%. The paper also explores the relationship between the precision of the transverse magnetic field estimate and the precision of the measurement of the total magnetic energy density, finding that the precision of the transverse magnetic field estimate should be comparable to that of the measurement of the total magnetic energy density, and that the precision of the measurement of the transverse magnetic field component should be comparable to that of the measurement of the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line of sight. The new correction method is useful for the use of vector magnetic field data in the study of solar flare source energies, as it provides a precision of 37% in the measurement of the energy density of solar flares, and it is also applicable to other solar physics research that involves the use of vector magnetic field data and remote sensing observations in the study of magnetized plasmas. The code used in this research is open to the public, and it is compatible with the SUNGRID computing cluster that is available to the solar physics research community in Canada. The new correction method has also been tested using observed data from the Solar Optical Observatory, and it is compatible with the instruments that are available at this facility, including the Broadband Imaging Telescope, the Vector Spectropolarimeter, and the Solar Optical Flux Instrument. The code used in this research can be used in the analysis of data from other solar facilities that are similar to the Solar Optical Observatory, including the Daniel K. Tackling the "Hubbard Sign Issue" is a challenge that complex-valued neural networks can help overcome by utilizing a separate unit to handle sign issues, specifically the Hubbard sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations. This approach allows for the estimation of physical observables in neural network learning, particularly in situations where the presence of a sign problem hinders traditional importance sampling methods. A recent advancement takes this idea a step further by developing a training algorithm for complex-valued neural networks that eliminates the need for a separate unit to handle the sign issue. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of this new approach for solving the Hubbard model on a 4x4 lattice and demonstrate that it not only manages the sign issue but also accurately estimates physical observables with error margins similar to traditional methods. Furthermore, this model exhibits robust performance across various simulation conditions and accurate results for physical observables even when the number of Monte Carlo samples is low. This network's simplicity, with only 156 complex-valued parameters, makes it an efficient tool for solving other sign problem scenarios in Monte Carlo simulations. This paper also presents a modified version of this network, with a more complex architecture, and shows that this model too can handle the sign issue and accurately estimate physical observables. This complex network's performance can be improved by incorporating a dropout mechanism in its training, which reduces the error in physical observable estimation. This paper's results highlight the vast potential of complex-valued neural networks in solving the sign problem issue in Monte Carlo simulations. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance cross-task generalization capabilities in massive language models by incorporating an unsupervised retrieval-based augmentation framework.
In this framework, we employ masked language modeling as an auxiliary task to refine the model during the adaptation process.
Retrieval augmentation draws on relevant prior experiences, represented by similar training samples, to present the model with novel instances.
We integrate these two techniques to create a dual-adaptation model, which exhibits significant improvements in addressing various text-based challenges.
Our proposed method surpasses various baselines in our experimental evaluation, which includes highly diverse text-based tasks such as conversational dialogue, sentence transduction, and stylistic transformation.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, the Chinese government launched a specialized team to counter misinformation. However, effective strategies for reducing speculation and controlling rumor spread speeds also raised scientific interests. To investigate the dynamics of rumor spread, spread speed was considered a key metric in research. Building on previous work, a mathematical model was developed to track changes in spread speed and measure influence by combining spread speed and duration. Empirical analysis of posts flagged as rumors on Sina Weibo during the COVID-19 period revealed that average spread speeds slowed substantially over time, from 5.7 hours on January 20th to 13.7 hours on February 15th, with average duration increasing from 13.8 hours to 14.8 hours over the same period. Furthermore, empirical research revealed that powered law models accurately captured the distribution of spread speeds and durations, allowing derivation of prevention and control priorities. Interestingly, results showed that among the powered law model parameters, the index that reflects the degree of dispersion has a more substantial impact on forecasted behaviors than the index that reflects influence, which is comparable to standard control indicators such as account ages. To enhance effectiveness of intervention strategies, powered law models can be employed as analytical tools to guide focused countermeasures, such as targeting short-lived, highly spreadable rumors or identifying influential users. While various technologies manage real-time and periodic processing efficiently, integrating them into seamless data flows remains a challenge. To address this issue, we have developed a proprietary industry use case that combines inflows and streams with periodic data integration. Unfortunately, this use case presents significant scalability issues that our research aims to address. We have designed and implemented LifeStream, a flow processing engine specifically tailored for periodic streams and ephemeral data. LifeStream's architecture, built around ring-based state persistence and efficient scheduling, enables fast and scalable performance. Our tests show that LifeStream achieves superior throughput and response times on real-world industry datasets when compared to leading stream processing engines and distributed batch processing systems. From a developmental perspective, LifeStream's unique architecture offers valuable insights into design trade-offs, particularly with regard to stream persistence and scheduling strategies, providing valuable lessons for developers building their own flow processing engines. We investigate the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, specifically focusing on the behavior of Pauli susceptibility $\chi$. Our calculations consider both the clean and dirty limit cases. In the clean limit, we calculate $\chi$ using a full band approach, while in the dirty limit, an $k$-space quasiclassical approximation is employed. Additionally, we calculate the overall magnetic energy $E_m$ for both limit cases. Our results show that the dirty limit case exhibits a $E_m \propto |m|^4$ behavior, in contrast to the $E_m \propto |m|^2$ pattern observed in clean limit case. This distinction in energy patterns may have experimental implications, in particular affecting the outcome of torque magnetometry within the dirty limit context. Furthermore, our calculations demonstrate that the superconducting gap closes more efficiently with increasing magnetization, which also has distinct signatures in various scattering patterns of Arkose scans. And finally, we observe a peculiar phenomenon in the dirty limit case, in which the Pauli susceptibility becomes negative within a particular magnetic orientation, in areas where the superconducting gaps are minimal. This negative susceptibility behavior is predicted to occur in specific areas near the edge of the mirror plane, which is further compounded by the fact that magneto-reflectivity experiments are sensitive to the angle of reflection mirrors, and therefore may fail to detect these negative susceptibility areas, which arise as a result of the nematic superconductivity environment. Which is not present in the clean limit case. In the clean limit context, our calculations also provide a more general expression for $\chi$, as well as the total magnetic energy $E_m$, in terms of the free electron parameter $g$. Which is equal to 2, according to experimental measurements, but is assumed to be $g=2.016$ in our calculations. And finally, we find that the total magnetic energy $E_m$ can be expressed as the product of the Pauli susceptibility $\chi$ and the square of the magnetization $m$, in the clean limit case. Which is further compounded by the fact that the superconducting gap closes more efficiently with increasing magnetization, in the clean limit context. Last but not least, we propose a simple yet effective approach to reduce the delay estimator's variance, which we demonstrate works for the aforementioned example. We investigate the quantum capacity and vacuum compressibility of quantum field theories in spacetime, considering thermal sources and treating spacetime as a quantum resource. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common-sense reasons both for and against performing various actions in specific situations. This dataset distinguishes itself from existing sources of common sense by focusing on the reasons behind actions, as seen in interactions between Wikipedia editors. We demonstrate that models incorporating reasons from ATOMIC about the same actions result in more accurate predictions than conventional methods. Furthermore, in a pioneering effort, we incorporate reasoning into dialogues by using ATOMIC to train and evaluate machine intelligence in a way that replicates the structure of CTO dialogues used to engage the Atomic Model. In a landmark finding, we discover that machine intelligence capable of responding to these dialogues significantly outperforms conventional methods, yielding a peak of 80% accuracy in predicting the actions discussed in CTO dialogues. This achievement is particularly notable given the challenging nature of CTO dialogues, as they necessitate the examination of 3500 disparate actions. Our investigation into machine intelligence that has been trained on if-then statements also uncovers intriguing findings, revealing that simply being informed about the world does not suffice to accurately predict the validity of individual statements. In a breakthrough, we demonstrate that by incorporating reasons from ATOMIC about the same actions, the accuracy of such machine intelligence exceeds that of conventional methods by a considerable margin. Our work on machine intelligence also yields a rich treasure of actionable guidelines for creating more reliable if-then statements. Ultimately, our investigation into the efficacy of models trained on if-then statements highlights the critical importance of incorporating reasons from ATOMIC about the same actions. Our proposed dataset and resulting discoveries are particularly relevant to renowned challenges in areas such as counterfactual reasoning and intent detection. Our findings and underlying technology are available at the website www.atomicdataset.com.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned transformations are reversible. To overcome these obstacles, this work proposes a novel bidirectional focus network that incorporates a spatial attention mechanism to adapt sampling rates and a reversible transformation to learn from speech and text data in both directions. By using this network in both encoder and decoder modes, it's possible to exchange the roles of input modalities, allowing for flexible design of multi-modal training protocols. This framework's capability to handle both unpaired text data and speech-only pre-training tasks makes it an attractive option for real-world ASR applications. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal that this model achieves a 6.0% reduction in word error rate (WER) only when trained on unpaired data, and a 12.6% decrease in WER when combining the speech and text datasets. Moreover, this work demonstrates that a carefully designed two-stage training protocol can further enhance performance, with a 20.3% decrease in WER compared to a baseline transducer model. The proposed model's simplicity, combined with its superior performance, makes it an appealing option for real-world ASR systems. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The paper also includes an exploratory analysis of two-dimensional parking scenarios. The most significant contribution of this paper to random walk theory is proving that there is a positive probability density function $\rho(x)$ such that the asymptotic density of $x$ in the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ is given by $\rho(x)$ for values of $x$ greater than some $x_0$, the threshold beyond which the first $k_n$ or the sum of the first $k_n$ parking locations exhibits a linear scaling. The paper shows that there is a constant $c$ such that the probability density function $\rho(x)$ is equal to $1/c$ for $x$ greater than some $x_0$, thereby solving the problem posed by Aldous and Diaconis.
