Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between respiratory aerosol emissions, aerosol transport, retention, and deposition. To quantify this risk, researchers use computational models that simulate the behavior of aerosols and estimate the likelihood of infection for individuals within the system. Previously, a full-scale, three-dimensional model has been developed to assess the spread of disease on a bus, considering various airflow and aerosol properties, and it has been compared to a simpler, statistically optimized model that utilizes a well-mixed framework. The results show that a state of equilibrium is achieved quickly, thereby justifying the use of the simpler model for real-world applications on buses. Furthermore, the inclusion of a discrete aerosol emission model into the statistically optimized framework has been explored, and its impact on the model's performance has been evaluated. The development of this model has also been made accessible through an online platform, where users can generate customized models and visualize the results graphically. The findings and the available toolkit have implications for predicting the transmission risk of various diseases on buses and similar confined environments. The research has been tailored to be relevant and accessible to a broad audience of transportation professionals, biomedical experts, and mathematicians. The associated methodology has been validated through comparison with existing research on the subject, and future research directions have been outlined. The associated toolkit is available online at https://github.com/amin-jav-an/. The associated methodology has also been previously published in the Journal of Computational Acoustics and the Journal of Aerosol Science. The investigation of spin-orbit interaction (SOI) beyond its local scope is a key area of study, particularly in controlling magnetic anisotropy through the spin-orbit proximity effect. To further understand and utilize this phenomenon, it is crucial to gain a clear and precise picture of how SOI influences the magnetic properties of materials with close interfaces, holding both ferromagnetic and heavy metal components. This study examines the relationship between interface interaction and the spin-orbit proximity effect in cobalt/bismuth multilayers through the variation of layer arrangement and temperature, thereby gaining insight into the underlying mechanisms. Findings show that the spin-orbit proximity effect leads to a significant reduction in the anisotropy of the outer Co layers when in direct contact with the heavy metal Bismuth, resulting in nearly isotropic magnetic anisotropy across these layers. Additionally, the absence of anisotropy temperature dependence in the middle Co layers suggests that the spin-orbit proximity effect can be stabilized in these layers even at higher temperatures, potentially enabling the creation of isotropic magnetic materials through the manipulation of layer structures. This research demonstrates the potential of heavy metal/ferromagnetic multilayers in designing complex magnetic materials with controlled anisotropy and exchange interaction. It also paves the way for exploring other heavy metal/ferromagnetic interface combinations to create unique magnetic properties that can be tailored for specific applications. This involves the Tb/Co system which displays an anisotropy enhancement due to fourfold crystal field, as well as the Gd/Co system which shows an anisotropy reduction caused by the exchange interaction, among many other possible combinations. This study opens a new pathway for investigating and developing novel magnetic materials with designed anisotropy and spin-orbit interaction, based on the spin-orbit proximity effect and interface interaction. It further suggests the utilization of heavy metal/ferromagnetic multilayers in magnetic tunnel junctions and other nanoscale magnetic devices. This research also implies potential applications of these materials in high density data storage and magnetic random access memory. It further highlights the possibility of exploring spin-orbit interaction in other systems, such as superconducting materials, topological insulators, and two-dimensional materials, which when combined with ferromagnetic components, can create complex two-way interaction between spin-orbit interaction and magnetic anisotropy, available for manipulation and with vast variety, potentially enabling the discovery of new phenomena and the development of cutting edge technologies. This study provides a foundation for these potential areas

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimization problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative regularization methods. Our findings were consistent across multiple settings, including image classification using CIFAR as well as language modeling. We were able to explain the performance improvement by identifying that enforcing Lipschitz continuity leads to improved robustness against perturbations and slight increases in model size. This resulted in better performance, although it fell short of expectations when comparing to models trained with large amounts of data. We also detailed several hyperparameter selection procedures that can be utilized to scale this approach to large datasets. In order to further investigate the performance of neural networks under different $p$-norms, we developed an analytical method that enables us to analyze the relationship between $p$-norms and the structure of neural networks. Through this analysis, we discovered specific $p$-norms that are sensitive to specific layers of a neural network. In conclusion, our research into enforcing Lipschitz continuity on neural networks was successful, and we believe this approach has significant potential as a regularization technique in machine learning. In particular, we think it has the potential to be effective in situations where robustness against input changes is critical. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zwang27/Lipschitz-Regularization. Our paper was previously published under a CC BY NC ND 2.1 license. Wang, Y. Chen, and X. Wang, which was published in the Proceedings of the 29th European Conference on Advances in Artificial Intelligence, page 7983-7993, 2020. Our findings regarding the performance of neural networks trained using the Lipschitz regularization framework on various datasets has been previously published in an unrelated paper titled "Lipschitz Regularization for Improved Neural Network Robustness" by Z. We investigate the production of high-mass dileptons in third-generation vector leptoquark models, focusing on the rare process of same-flavor Drell-Yan production. Our analysis is performed at the next-to-leading order in QCD, combined with parton shower evolution, and accounts for the impact of subprocesses involving the gauge vector leptoquarks interacting with gluons and quark-gluon fields. Furthermore, we calculate the formalism's applicability limits, finding that the rare nature of this process makes it particularly sensitive to vector leptoquark masses. Specifically, at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, we find that the $e^+e^-$ and $\mu^+\mu^-$ Drell-Yan dilepton mass distributions become less discriminatory as the mass of the vector leptoquark increases above 400 GeV and 700 GeV, respectively. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that same-flavor Drell-Yan production serves as a highly sensitive probe for the existence and characterization of third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks, especially at the future 100 TeV collider. There, we find that the discovery threshold for a vector leptoquark with charge $\pm 5/3$ can be as low as 4.5 TeV, given a statistical significance of 10 and assuming all possible decay modes are accessible. Our comprehensive predictions are made available through an easily accessible code posted online. The code generates raw data suitable for further numerical analysis with specialized event reconstruction tools. The generated code expands upon existing vector leptoquark simulations, enhancing their capability to handle higher-order QCD corrections and providing a more accurate description of Drell-Yan production in the transition region, where the vector leptoquark mass approaches and exceeds the squared mass of the incoming partons. The code has a straightforward structure, consisting of an initial section that defines constant values, followed by a section describing the integration variables and their respective ranges, and finally a section detailing the output variables and their calculation procedures. The code is compatible with the HERMINATOR interpreter, upon which it relies to perform the integrations required for the NLO calculations. The raw data produced by the code consists of sets of output variables, each set corresponding to a single event defined by the integration variables. These sets are organized into tables with a clear format, demonstrating the compatibility of the code with popular event reconstruction tools that can utilize the raw data to perform further analysis. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, while also providing a quality score for each image. We evaluated this model on three separate datasets, utilizing PET scans with different doses and scan durations, and demonstrated its capability to enhance images with a 50% reduction in dose or a 30% reduction in scan time to image quality equivalent to standard doses or scan times. The results were consistently verified through blinded ratings by radiologists. This model has the potential to minimize PET scan doses and durations while maintaining reliable image quality, as validated by radiologists. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/alumatherani/uncertain-neural-pet.

The center of a mention refers to the most important entity to which it is linked in a text. This concept has significant implications for understanding the relationships between mentions, and it has been employed in various operations of neural coreference systems. To date, research has focused on utilizing center-related information without addressing the underlying principles of centering theory. This study investigates the connection between the structure of neural coreference systems and the principles of centering theory, examining how the interaction of mentions affects the relationship between a mention and its alleged center. To achieve this, we analyzed the outputs of pre-trained coreference systems using a suite of measures derived from centering theory. Our findings reveal that the relationship between mentions and their centers can vary, depending on the context of the text, and that the center of a mention is often linked to its nominal subject or to the main clause in which it resides. Furthermore, measures of centering can be utilized to assess the performance of neural coreference systems, providing a tool with which researchers can explore the dynamics of text and coreference relationships. Our research was conducted using a system trained on the ALLEGRO dataset, and our results show that the measures developed in this study reflect the underlying principles of centering theory and can be linked to various operations of neural coreference systems. Our analysis highlights the complexities of coreference relationships and suggests that neural systems trained on a single dataset may struggle with the diverse contexts of centering theory. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, the estimation of ranges using WiFi signals without fingerprinting data is also common and employs machine learning models to estimate distances based on signal strength indicators. In this research, a novel algorithm is presented that leverages a specific WiFi-based estimation technique called Received Signal Strength Indicator averaging, to estimate locations. A critical examination of this algorithm's performance in relation to well-established methods such as fingerprinting-based localization and range estimation, reveals its key advantages. Moreover, the results obtained from our experiments conducted in two distinct indoor environments, demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this algorithm. The findings show that this algorithm's performance surpasses that of conventional methods including a widely used open-source localization tool called iAMAP, in both tested environments. The evaluation used a range estimation error metric called Mean Absolute Error, to compare the performance of this algorithm against that of established methods, and revealed its superior performance in relation to these standards. The results presented herein also highlight the significance of proper configuration, including the number of RSSI samples and the scanning interval, in ensuring optimal performance. The research was conducted using a low-cost WiFi device, which is widely accessible to the academic community. The data collected and the code for this research have been made available online for further development and experimentation by interested researchers. The algorithm's performance was also analyzed in a real-world setting, at a university library, and the results showed that this approach is practical and effective in locating individuals. The research highlights the possibility of deploying this algorithm in similar indoor environments without the need for costly setup and configuration, as required by other localization methods. The results also showed that the algorithm's performance decreases when there are obstacles in the environment, which is also analyzed in a separate experiment. The research was conducted using a low-frequency bandwidth, which is widely available in indoor settings, and the results showed that the algorithm's performance increases when the bandwidth is higher. The research was also conducted to analyze the impact of moving speed on the accuracy of the algorithm, and the results showed that the algorithm's performance decreases when the moving speed is higher. The research was conducted to analyze the impact of different machine learning models on the algorithm's performance, and the results showed that the performance of the model presented herein is the best among the models tested. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling design, particle bunch characteristics, and radio-frequency cavity design on beam breakup instability. This paper explores the relationship between cavity design and beam breakup instability, focusing on the effect of filling design, and reveals that the threshold for beam breakup instability is linked to the average beam current and can be anticipated by a critical current criterion. Nevertheless, due to the complexity of RCAs, partially filled beam waves can cause beam breakup instability, potentially leading to premature cessation of operations. To enhance the stability at high currents, researchers suggest placing deflecting RF cavities at the end of beam pulses, where the beam is most sensitive to acceleration, and advancing front bunches, which could further reduce beam breakup instability by limiting interaction between adjacent beam pulses. By adopting these measures, researchers believe that beam breakup instability can be overcome as an limiting factor in energy recovery linacs, allowing for the use of existing facilities with increased scientific and technological advancements. The findings mentioned above originated from research conducted at the Brookhaven Linear Accelerator System and the Advanced Photon Source. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. In both limits, the two-gluon CEV exhibits helicity non-conservation and displays color-stripping properties equivalently to single-emission CEVs. Notably, in both limits, the two-gluon CEV can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, single-emission CEVs, and cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. In the MRK limit, this representation simplifies to a form that facilitates connection to reggeised single-emission amplitudes, via a residue that is a product of two Witten indices. In the NMRK limit, this representation allows extension of six-gluon amplitude functions to include all-helicity configurations, achieving achievability of NNLL accuracy for such amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As a byproduct, the calculation yields a novel expression for a specific BFKL six-gluon amplitude in the NMRK limit, equivalently to the form proposed in [1], but derived using a different approach. Moreover, the analysis reveals a misidentification of a cross ratio in [2], for which an alternative labelling is suggested. Finally, the analysis also yields a dispersive part for a specific BFKL six-gluon amplitude in the MRK limit, equivalently to the form proposed in [3], but derived using a different approach. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the accuracy of these models has been limited to rectangular and circular shapes. A new study develops a mathematical approach based on the strong stretching theory, enabling the analysis of shaped brushes with any form. By combining this approach with the strong stretching theory, researchers found that the models can be unified and applicable exclusion areas identified. Additionally, the study's results are applicable to flat surfaces and reveals a universal brush region that can be precisely defined. Furthermore, in cases where the grafting density is low, the study demonstrates that its effect is insignificant. In all scenarios, the strong stretching theory proves to be highly accurate. In addition, the study provides a critical examination of previously proposed models, including those for branched and dendrimer structures. One such model, proposed by Birshtein and Pavlikova, is specifically re-examined in this study. A numerical validation of the new approach for various shapes, including triangular, square, and parabolic shapes, is also presented in the study. A key finding of the study is that the strong stretching theory's applicability is limited to shapes that can be categorized as narrow shapes with a small aspect ratio. On the other hand, shapes with a large aspect ratio require alternative models, such as the de Gennes model. In such cases, the exclusion area becomes significantly larger than the predicted value of one brush height squared. In fact, in cases where the shape is elongated, the exclusion area can be as large as nine brush heights squared. In cases where the surface topography is complex, with varied shapes and sizes, the study suggests that the exclusion area can be calculated by taking the average of all shapes, provided that the majority of the shapes have a small aspect ratio. In contrast, shapes with a large aspect ratio will still require alternative models. In addition to surface-grafted polymers, the study's results are also applicable to the core-microgel complexation scenario, where the exclusion area is determined by the ratio of the core to the gel height. In this scenario, the exclusion area changes from one brush height squared to nine brush heights squared as the ratio increases from a small to a large aspect ratio. The metric dimension of a graph is a concept originally developed to describe the spatiotemporal localization of an object within a metric space. This idea has been extended to graphs, where a set of vertices represents observers with unique identifiers, and the goal is to determine the minimum number of nodes required to accurately identify all vertices in the graph. We introduce a new parameter, called the trimmed metric dimension, which removes edges with a length of one from consideration. We examine the relationship between traditional metric dimension and this new variant, and determine that the trimmed metric dimension can be any integer greater than or equal to half the number of vertices in the graph, or if the graph is connected and has a diameter of two, then its trimmed metric dimension is either one or equals the number of vertices in the graph. We also calculate the trimmed metric dimension for specific graphs, and demonstrate that it can be computed using the metric dimension and graph parameters. Furthermore, we establish upper and lower bounds for the trimmed metric dimension, and provide examples to demonstrate that these bounds are tight. Lastly, we determine the trimmed metric dimension for random geometric graphs, and compare it to the number of nodes in the graph. We then outline some open problems related to this new parameter. The concepts and results presented in this paper are accompanied by suitable examples and illustrations. We hope that these results will help researchers from various fields, such as discrete mathematics, computer science, and network optimization, among others. The concept of trimmed metric dimension can be applied to real-world scenarios involving networks, such as smart cities, biological systems, and transportation systems. The development of specific algorithms to calculate the trimmed metric dimension for general graphs remains an ongoing challenge. The trimmed metric dimension can be calculated for random geometric graphs, but there are many open questions related to this topic, such as determining the asymptotic value of the trimmed metric dimension for a specific type of random geometric graph, or establishing an upper bound for the trimmed metric dimension of another type of random geometric graph. Researchers explored a novel approach in the image processing of Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope data, focusing on all-sky maps and source variability. By employing a machine learning-based technique, they successfully reduced background noise and enhanced the detection of rare, variable sources. A comparison with traditional methods revealed this approach can be more effective in identifying sources, particularly those with periodic or massive variable patterns. This technique's potential advantages were demonstrated by re-analyzing data from sources known to vary, and it has implications for searching the data for sources with predicted patterns of variability, such as axion stars or rotating neutron stars. To apply this method on a larger scale, a more advanced version of the algorithm is needed to handle larger data sets efficiently. This project highlights the creative uses of machine learning for astrophysical research and demonstrates a potential method for finding variable sources, often characterized by sources with isolated gamma-ray loci, specifically in the direction of the Milky Way center. The underlying algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub.

The concept of a monarchy in combinatorial optimization has its roots in various fields, providing a useful abstraction and efficient algorithms for solving complex problems. A key property of a monarchy is that it arranges objects in a hierarchical structure, with each higher-level object incorporating information from lower-level ones, and accurately reflects the underlying instance structure. This property enables faster-than-naive solutions for various problems, including maximizing the total reward, distributing items, and scheduling tasks. However, a significant limitation of monarchies is that their construction requires access to the original input, which can be difficult to obtain in certain scenarios. Building on the monarchy framework, we introduce a new concept, the serial monarchy, which addresses this issue and can be constructed from scratch using only the optimization black box. Additionally, we establish that a serial monarchy yields an efficient algorithm for solving various discrete optimization problems, and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of this framework by applying it to random instances of two specific problems. In our analysis of present large language models, we observed that generating counterfactual descriptions between two sentences, such as replacing the subject of a sentence, primarily focuses on developing related phrasal hypotheses, rather than predicting entire counterfactual sentences. To demonstrate the significance of phrasal counterfactual hypotheses, we presented a novel task called DISCO, where given a sentence, participants choose the most suitable counterfactual description among several options. Our findings show that models pre-trained on text alone excel at this task, and the performance can be further enhanced by fine-tuning small networks. Additionally, we found that training a text generator on phrasal counterfactual hypotheses generated by a large language model by playing a game of "fill-in-the-blank" improves the diversity of generated descriptions. In a second experiment, we demonstrated that training a text generator on these hypotheses enhances its ability to produce more realistic counterfactual sentences when given a set of possible descriptions. Our work offers several applications, including but not limited to text generation, where producing high-quality counterfactual sentences is necessary. We hope our research encourages other researchers to explore the possibilities of phrasal counterfactual hypotheses within large language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/nytng/disco.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating networks that generate multiple classes with specific conditions proves difficult, as it requires training the generator on a single sample for multiple classes, which goes against the principle of efficient training inherent to conditional GANs.  We propose an innovative technique to generate multi-label samples from conditional GANs trained on single positive labels.  This technique leverages the existing networks to generate samples with a single positive label and a hidden latent representation, which can be used to generate additional labels.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique by utilizing a network trained on lung nodules on a CT dataset and generating samples with both nodule and metastasis labels.  The generated data proves comparable to human radiologists, as evaluated by both medical specialists and machine learning models.  Furthermore, these generated samples enhance the robustness of machine learning models when subjected to common attacks, such as FGSM and L2.  We also explore the application of this technique to real-world datasets and outline possible future developments.  The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghoul333/SP2ML.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of sound recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of noise-resistant and device-agnostic algorithms for cardiac sound classification.  From the 13 heart sounds collected from the PhysioNet dataset, 5-short long segments were derived, resulting in 65 segments after quality control.  Experimental techniques included evaluating 9 features across 3 noise types and 3 recording distances, as well as the performance of 3 machine learning classifiers under different noise levels and recording distances.  The findings show that entropy-based features demonstrate the highest sensitivity to habitus sounds, while the SVR classifier reveals superior performance across various noise levels and recording distances.  The established model's performance was then tested on a larger dataset composed of 132 short segments, yielding a 70% accuracy rate.  The research provides a foundation for creating cardiac auscultation tools that are insensitive to background noise and the recording device used, and its findings have significant implications for the design of such systems.  In addition, the study's results can be used to create a simple, robust cardiac sound classification system based on machine learning techniques.  The proposed approach can also serve as a framework for evaluating and selecting suitable features and classifiers for other cardiac sound analysis tasks.  The development of noise-resistant models has the potential to improve the efficacy of cardiac auscultation for detecting hyperopia and other heart conditions, and may be applied to various medical surveillance contexts, including hospital settings, at home, or during physical activity.  The research's methodology can be adapted for use with other sound-based diagnosis techniques, such as lung sound analysis.  The proposed model's efficacy in managing noise and device variability has been consistently demonstrated across different evaluation methods, which further enhances its value to the scientific community.  The study's findings on the importance of entropy-based features, along with the performance of the SVR classifier, and the proposed framework's suitability for evaluating features and classifiers, among others, offer valuable insights that can be applied to various other cardiac sound analysis tasks.  The development of models like the one presented can be viewed as a way to create a "golden ear" that is insensitive to noise and device variability, with the potential to overcome the limitations of human auscultation.  The research provides a foundation for creating a perfect cardiac auscultation tool

We have theoretically analyzed multiple aspects of laser-induced three-body recombination from spinless dimer states, which can be realized using atom-molecule trapping systems with a 1D configuration. This process is precise and efficiently converts spinful atoms into molecules with the same parity as the initial dimer state. Our calculations demonstrate various relevant coefficients for different initial state conditions. Furthermore, our model assumes that the binding energy of the dimer is negligible, allowing an approximation of spinless dimer states as a superposition of two photons. This leads to a key innovation - an atom-molecule interaction term that involves a large number of photons can now be accessed through this recombination channel. This previously hidden interaction effect could potentially steer quantum trajectories in trapping systems. Our findings also highlight the significance of initial state broadening, as it leads to an increase in the efficiency of recombination, as well as affecting the coefficients of laser-induced three-body recombination. Initially, this efficiency increase results from initial state broadening, but it eventually leads to a decline as the broadening becomes more significant and the efficient recombination occurs within a smaller trapping region. This, in turn, causes the efficient recombination of a higher number of atoms into molecules, but with a reduced coefficient. Our analysis has been focused on a 1D configuration, but our results can be extended to higher dimensional systems. Causal deep learning, a branch within the causal machine learning framework, aims to produce accurate predictions by accounting for the effects of prior events on current observations. This field has seen significant growth, leading to various methods for constructing relevant variables and estimating relationships. However, there is still no established theory to gauge the performance of these methods and ensure that learned models are free from bias. In contrast to non-causal deep learning, which relies heavily on modeling the probability distribution of the data, causal deep learning places more emphasis on modeling the underlying mechanisms and relationships. We highlight three key aspects of causal deep learning: (1) modeling the connection between variables, (2) identifying treatment effects, and (3) dealing with selection biases. We also examine three popular methods that fit into these categories. Although causal deep learning offers numerous benefits, using these methods requires careful consideration of potential issues, such as overparameterization and the risk of bias in models learned from selected data. We present an open-ended challenge in this paper, i.e., developing valid performance metrics for causal deep learning. We discuss the implications of this problem for various applications and offer a sample solution for the case of overfitting. Lastly, we conclude by outlining future research directions in causal deep learning.

This study conducts a comprehensive comparison of state-of-the-art algebraic solvers for finite element models of cardiac mechanics. We examined and compared the performance of four multilevel preconditioners: PARDISO as a solo competitor, and three other methods that combine PARDISO with two-factor and algebraic multigrid solvers, and a third combination of PARDISO with two-factor and GMRES. Our analysis was done using separate sets of realistic simulation data and modeling parameters, and we evaluated the solutions using multiple criteria including iteration numbers, solution times, and error metrics. Our findings showed that the most high-performance models, which exhibited balanced performance in terms of computational speed and solution accuracy, used PARDISO coupled with two-factor or ALBERT solvers. Specifically, we observed that the two-factor solver produced more balanced results when the material models involved stress-dependent diffusion, whereas the ALBERT solver yielded superior outcomes in models featuring structurally heterogeneous left ventricle tissues. On the other hand, the two-factor solver outperformed the ALBERT solver in models incorporating electrophysiological components. Our research underpins the significance of solver selection based on model characteristics and highlights possible pathways to further optimization, such as enhancing the flexibility of algebric multigrid solvers and two-factor solvers to better accommodate various levels of spatial discretization elements. Lastly, our study highlights the value of accessible access to high-end computing hardware, specifically the NEURON-HOCN cluster, in achieving these results. Ultimately, our findings have broader implications for solving large-scale biomechanical models of various organ systems. Complex systems consisting of multiple interconnected components typically follow dynamic laws that connect the system's overall state to a unified objective such as optimization or a critical threshold. Traditional machine learning approaches typically isolate individual components and model their internal dynamics, as opposed to modeling the system as a whole. In this work, a novel framework is established that leverages graph neural networks to learn the underlying dynamics of complex systems, focusing on multi-agent reinforcement learning as a key application. By aggregating node representations, a graph neural network learns an integrated state representation that meets a predefined criterion, and this representation is used in conjunction with a critic network to enhance the efficiency of reinforcement learning. The proposed framework and representation learning approach are demonstrated in a simulation of multi-agent reinforcement learning, along with real-world experiments in mobility management and market mechanisms. The results show that this approach outperforms traditional approaches in tasks involving complex interactions among components. We establish a formula for counting specific combinations of partitions that arise from interpreting properties in homotopy theory, utilizing the concept of Frobenius groups and a connection to the Coxeter numbers. This formula is expressed through the use of a specialized function called the q-Poincaré polynomial, which is a comprehensive statistical model with adjustable parameters. By manipulating this polynomial, we identify key intervals in which the number of combinations exceeds a given value, in addition to determining the minimum and maximum values the number of combinations can take. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the number of combinations decreases as the complexity of the model increases, and we identify a critical point at which the number of combinations becomes negative, thereby losing mathematical significance. The proposed model also provides lower and upper bounds for counting another type of combination called the descent set, which is known to be challenging to calculate using conventional methods. The results presented in this paper were previously known in limited cases, whereas the new approach offers a unified and comprehensive proof for these cases. The proposed method involves a complex mathematical construction that utilizes the concept of a Bruhat order and a partition system, allowing us to translate the problem of counting combinations into a simpler form that can be calculated using the Poincaré polynomial. This construction is a novel extension of the original approach introduced by Ethan Leuin, which only considered a single element rather than the entire partition system. The results presented in this paper have been verified through numerical simulation using adjustable parameters, which showed that the proposed model provides a reasonably accurate estimate of the number of combinations despite some overestimation. The paper also includes two appendices that provide additional technical details about the constructed polynomial and the relation between the Poincaré polynomial and the descent set. The results presented in this paper have numerous applications in mathematics and computer science, including group theory, algebraic geometry, theoretical computer science, and biology. The proposed method offers a general framework for solving problems involving counting and constructing arbitrary combinations of partitions, which can be applied to a wide range of problems in these fields. Creating realistic virtual injuries for human heads is a challenging task that requires significant artistic experience and technical expertise. Traditional approaches rely heavily on human input to define desired characteristics of the generated images, which can limit the creativity and realism of outcomes. To address this, we develop a innovative method using progressive variational adversarial networks that automatically creates realistic and varied head images with controlled injury features. This approach enables real-world applications such as virtual product testing and realistic special effects for film production. We demonstrate this method's utility by generating 20 different types of head injury images. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/zwang84/Brain-Injury-Synthesis.

These varied approaches converge into a unifying framework, which can be viewed from either an optimization or a network architecture perspective. The framework's flexibility allows multiple contrastive learning techniques to be integrated using different combination methods, such as model combination, network combination, and weighted averaging. The proposed unifying structure provides a solid theoretical foundation for many existing architectures, and its computational efficiency has been demonstrated across a range of applications, including residual learning, bridge learning, and hybrid learning. Working with categorical data for model selection and feature reduction becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires the estimation and comparison of multiple logistic regressions. The Group Lasso has been a useful tool for such tasks, but its application to categorical data is hindered by its restrictive assumption that all observations within a group belong to the same class, which can be visually explored but isn't necessarily true. We introduce a new technique, the Generalized Group Fused Lasso, that takes into account the diversity of categorical data, allowing different observations to have distinct classes while still facilitating comparison and selection based on model fit. Unlike other methods, it avoids sparsity within individual groups and provides a more interpretable and simpler solution than other generalized group Lasso techniques. We also provide a comprehensive comparison of our method to other models, demonstrating through simulated and real-world data how The Generalized Group Fused Lasso outperforms existing techniques in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. We apply this method to high-dimensional categorical data in the biomedical field and show its flexibility and versatility in other domains. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, these models struggle with events and entities that lie outside their training data, such as unknown events or entities with rare names. To address this challenge, we introduce a method that incorporates structured knowledge into these models, enabling them to effectively handle unfamiliar situations. Specifically, we utilize existing information structures, such as Knowledge Graphs, to train LLMs that can recognize and respond to diverse events and entities. To accommodate dynamic knowledge, we develop a method that adapts existing optimization techniques for relational learning, leveraging graph neural networks to capture complex relationships between entities. In evaluating this method, we created customized evaluation environments that mimic real-world settings, incorporating both synthetic and actual knowledge graphs. Our findings show that LLMs trained with structured knowledge exhibit a 6% improvement in accuracy when dealing with named entities and a 25% boost in accuracy with action description scenarios. Moreover, this method demonstrates notable efficiency, with a mere 2% increase in computation required for model training. Our code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/THUHLSL/SKILL.

A double annealing schedule is proposed to adapt a a an autoencoder-based pre-training method for deriving initial model weights, resulting in the DPCRN model. Initially, the model weighs noise and clean signal equally, then gradually shifts its focus towards prioritizing the clean signal as it learns from available noisily recorded data. The proposed DPCRN model achieves top ranking in deep neural network-based evaluation considering room impulse response and far-field recording conditions, and also outperforms existing models in other conditions. Additionally, a simplified version of the model called SCPN, which drops the t-DCN module, ranks highly in evaluation considering babble background noise. A nonlinear charged black hole in an anti-de Sitter spacetime is analyzed to determine if it exhibits heat transfer due to shading, a phenomenon initially predicted by Firouzjaee and Ghodsi. Our calculation shows that indeed, there is a heat flux from the black hole to its surroundings, which can be categorized based on the shading angle. Our results also demonstrate that this heat flux meets the criteria of which direction it flows, as it always moves from the black hole to its surroundings, thus not being influenced by the sign of the cosmological constant. Our calculation of the heat flux is accomplished through the use of a nonlinear equation relating charge and spacetime distance, which results in the heat flux being proportional to this distance. Our findings are further verified by analyzing two specific nonlinear charge configurations: one in which the heat flux is proportional to both the shading angle and the distance between the black hole and the charge, and another in which the heat flux is proportional to the square of the shading angle, although in this case it's dependent on the assumption that the charge is minimal. Our research on the shade thermodynamics of a nonlinear charged Anti-de Sitter black hole adds two new cases to the existing list of heat transfer configurations. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the extensive amount of data required. Multiple methods exist for state reconstruction, including those utilizing specific system properties, such as entanglement or synchronization behavior. This study proposes an integrated approach to state reconstruction that takes into account the changes in entanglement and onset of synchronization, and is applicable to both open and closed systems. A combined measure of entanglement and synchronization, based on the Wigner function, is introduced and its relationship to the state tomogram is established. The findings can be applied to integrated systems, providing direct access to the state information through measurement of radiation tomograms. Furthermore, the integrated measure enables discussion of system properties at different preparation parameters, thereby allowing for the identification of suitable conditions for, for example, teleportation or quantum computation. The integrated approach is demonstrated through the calculation of alteration in entanglement and onset of synchronization for a cavity with coupling to a Markovian environment, as well as an open system, based on the radiation field itself. The findings are compared with the respective system's long-term average state, thereby validating the approach. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of systems, from the radiation field to superconducting qubits, as well as to systems with different environment settings, ending at systems with random noise. The integrated approach is complemented by a discussion on the alteration in entanglement and onset of synchronization at different rotation parameters, as well as the condition for suitable condition preparation, thereby enabling the selection of suitable state preparations for, for example, entanglement formation or computation. 360-degree virtual tourism videos provide engaging and interactive views of diverse tourist locations but present a significant challenge in predicting the viewer's perspective due to their intricate structure and vast amount of available data. In response to this difficulty, many deep learning approaches have been developed, resulting in several classification scenarios such as separating foreground and background, classifying object categories, and distinguishing between front and back perspectives. However, these tasks do not take into account the crucial aspect of user experience, which is determined by the relationship between perspective and video content, including sound and titles. In this paper, we propose an innovative method that utilizes video subtitles in addition to audio and video streams to predict the viewer's perspective. By integrating the information from subtitles with their standard classification, our method's results show significant improvements in accuracy to 92.5% in a simple experiment setup and 88.1% in a more complex Google Tour format setup. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates practical value by incorporating experience-based subtitles for specific locations. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/Chenyu-890924/360-degree-Perspective-Prediction.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution, denoted as $G_{TMD}(x)$, is examined. This function, part of the TMD factorization framework, is particularly useful in describing hard scattering processes involving protons or nuclei. The underlying theory, due to small-x phenomena, relies heavily on nonlinear effects from quantum chromodynamics. As a result, $G_{TMD}(x)$ is expressed as a double integral, one of which is related to the gluon condensate, which enters as a non-perturbative parameter in this context. However, this integration introduces an infrared renormalon that can be observed as an asymmetrical peak in a weighted measurement of $G_{TMD}(x)$ at small values of x. A crucial finding of this research is that the inclusion of this renormalon leads to an x-dependent shift specifically related to the Borel transform of the condensate, which can be quantitatively assessed. In examining processes involving photons and jets in deep-inelastic scattering off protons at small x, the induced shift is demonstrated to have a tangible impact on the measurement of $G_{TMD}(x)$, with effects observable at values of x as large as 0.01. Furthermore, this study underlines the significance of incorporating infrared renormalons in TMD distributions and highlights the potential utility of proton Drellýn scattering at small x as well as other processes involving jets and photons in deep-inelastic scattering. The introduced x-dependent shift provides a precise, quantifiable impact of the infrared renormalon that can be observed in weighted measurements of $G_{TMD}(x)$ and generally applies to other TMD distributions involving gluons, although it was specifically derived in this research. The results presented in this paper were obtained through numerical computations, and the associated TMD factorization framework includes references to underlying theoretical papers. A black-box model can be utilized to provide knowledge for a target task by making decisions on a separate dataset, without requiring access to its features or predictions. We investigate the possibility of knowledge transfer in a zero-shot setting, where the model's decisions on a diverse range of tasks offer valuable information. Our primary goal is to determine whether we can effectively train a model on these decisions to achieve competitive performance compared to training it on the original data. Our key contribution involves introducing two approaches that enable model performance on a target task after experiencing a black-box model's decisions on a diverse range of tasks. Our results show that it is possible to train a model on the basis of these decisions alone. We also conduct an in-depth analysis of the factors influencing the model's performance and find that both the diversity of tasks and the relationship between the target and source tasks have a significant impact on performance. We demonstrate this in a zero-shot setting using a dataset of 50 tasks and show that performance improves when considering more diverse tasks and provide intuitive reasons for this behavior. We further show that knowledge transfer is possible even when the target and source tasks are identical, as we would intuitively expect. We also explore different approaches of selecting a subset of tasks that are more diverse and find that the proposed greedy algorithm leads to better performance compared to a random subset. We demonstrate our approach against a suite of baselines and show that our method achieves a higher level of performance compared to the state-of-the-art approaches. We are confident that our results offer a promising direction for solving the problem of task diversity. We also discuss the possible connections between our approach and other techniques such as meta-learning and show that there is promise in integrating our approach with these techniques. We provide our code at https://github.com/abhinav-26/Zero-Shot-Knowledge-Transfer.

Understanding the efficacy of imitation learning for various tasks is crucial, however this approach often relies on an expert to provide demonstrations, which can be time consuming, expensive and sometimes impossible to obtain.  In order to make imitation learning more practical and accessible, this study explores the feasibility of employing co-training, an approach that leverages concurrently available, non-expert data, combined with both models and the knowledge they possess, to enhance both models and thereby the imitation learning process.  To address this challenge, the paper proposes a novel co-imitation training method that utilizes non-expert data and incorporates a contrastive learning technique to mitigate any potential deterioration of model performance.  The proposed approach is thoroughly evaluated and compared to the current imitation learning methods, and its effectiveness demonstrated across a range of tasks, including language models, dense linear classification, and generative models.  The results show that the co-imitation training method is not only capable of handling partially reliable experts but also outperforms the current imitation learning methods when expert demonstrations are available.  The proposed approach is further applied to the challenging domain adaptation task, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance. Evaluating the best action space size for reinforcement learning-based neural machine translation remains unclear, as both discrete word-level and action-probability-based methods have their own strengths and limitations. To address this issue, we investigate reinforcement learning with extensive action spaces of various sizes, taking into account the trade-off between diversity and coherence. Our key finding indicates that larger action spaces initially enhance coherence but eventually compromise diversity. To overcome this limitation, we develop a novel threshold-based strategy, restricting selected actions to a minimal set that meet a quality standard, thus maintaining coherence while increasing the chance of discovering high-quality actions, as demonstrated in our experiments. This approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing the difficulty of difficulty exploitation. Our work is applicable to a range of tasks, including summarization and dialogue generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/RL-NMT/tree/action_probing. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, depending on the circumstances, they may achieve a non-equilibrium steady
state, where continuous exchange of energy and information with the surroundings is
balanced and where periodic fluctuations are stabilized forever. The theory of such systems
can get very complicated, necessitating extensive computational efforts to predict
parabolic curves of heating, fermionization, and other non-trivial phenomena.
Experimental verification of these predictions is made feasible by using a controlled
and periodic driving force on a single quantum system, in this case a qubit driven by
a periodic signal via an optical cavity, which allows for efficient and precise measurement of essential parameters of the system. A unique feature of this system is that it can shift to a non-equilibrium steady state, where energy is continuously input and output at different rates, manageable through adjustable elements of the setup. Our experimental findings match the theoretical predictions and display a fascinating behavior in which the width of a peak in the spectrum shifts dramatically as the driving frequency is changed, yet remains stable over time, allowing for precise comparison with the theoretical curves. Furthermore, this system provides a versatile platform for validating general principles that apply to open quantum systems in non-equilibrium conditions, as well as a practical means of implementing quantum thermal machines that can generate controlled amounts of work and heat from a single energy source. The degree of overlap between the experimental and theoretical results suggests possible avenues for enhancing the system, such as using a reflective mirror with a higher finesse, which could reveal more complex phenomena like periodic heating and cooling, demultiplexing and fermionization, among others. Specifically, we examine the implications of a hypersurface being recurrent under different definitions, and investigate the relationship between biharmonic hypersurfaces and harmonic operators. Furthermore, we discuss the integral and local properties of biharmonic hypersurfaces, and the role of vector fields in these properties. The paper also considers the specific case of mean curvature, and provides a formula for its integral in relation to a hypersurface's mean curvature operator. The final section discusses some open research problems related to biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space. Given any real number p greater than 1 and any integer q greater than 1, this paper defines a new notion called p/q-identifiable sets within the context of number theory, specifically within the realm of integer arrays and quadratic forms. It then demonstrates the connection between these sets and a particular class of functions known as L-functions, which includes Dirichlet's character function as a subset. Furthermore, it establishes criteria for these sets to be considered comprehensive or minimal, and also demonstrates that in many instances, these sets can be proven to be equivalent in measure to a specific segment of the number line, which in the case of p equal to 2, simplifies to showing they are capable of identifying all algebraic numbers. Additionally, it provides a more in depth analysis of both 1/2-identifiable and 2/3-identifiable sets, which reveals that the former includes the set of algebraic numbers, while the latter is capable of identifying a specific class of quadratic fields. Lastly, it concludes by discussing the potential connection between these sets and a problem known as the Littlewood conjecture.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for strong consistency, quorum consistency, and apollo consistency settings.  For transactional coherence, MongoDB uses the "patchable causal" model.  In this paper, a specification for transactional coherence is presented and patchable causal defined as a subset of this specification.  Furthermore, a methodology for verifying coherence models is proposed, incorporating a graph theory-based approach to safely extend the specification.  This methodology was applied to MongoDB, which currently lacks a formal description.  Therefore, a formal description of MongoDB was developed and verified to enforce the patchable causal coherence model.  This development also discovered issues with MongoDB's current implementation, specifically regarding snapshot readability and the handling of concurrent writes to the same document.  These problems led to small, contained patches being applied to MongoDB's source code.  This paper is the first to present a formal description and verification of MongoDB's coherence model.  Additionally, research has been conducted into various consistency settings and their corresponding coherence models, which were also formally described and verified.  These descriptions demonstrate that MongoDB's available consistency settings, including strong consistency, can be achieved through appropriate configurations of its coherence model.  This may be applied to allow for patchable coherence.  Such patches would enable research into the interaction between consistency settings and coherence model configurations, as well as allow for the verification of future modifications to MongoDB's coherence model. By combining geometric theory with dynamics, a concealed structure called the conduction metric is generated, which directly influences the assembly's behavior and can even predict whether the system will remain stable or switch to a different state. Utilizing conduction metrics, we developed an integrated model that explores the interplay between individual components and the complex geometry of a network, consisting of nodes that represent the elements, edges that represent interactions between them, and geodesics that represent the assembly's spatial configuration. We applied this integrated model to nanoscale assemblies consisting of hydrogen bonds, which link pairs of molecules into a network, in addition to triangle-based interactions that connect three molecules to form a triangle. By simulating these assemblies, we found that the integrated model accurately predicts the assembly's stability or the time it takes for the assembly to change state, even when the condition changes suddenly. The integrated model and conduction metrics can be applied to a wide range of complex networks, including biological networks, financial systems, transport systems, social networks, and the brain, among many others. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from the Solar Wind Electromagnetic Investigation suite on board the Parker Solar Probe during its first 12 orbits. The investigations focused on energy flux patterns and how they vary in response to changing solar radiation. The research revealed that the energy flux slows down at the same rate as the solar wind speed when looking at overall trends but speeds up again when considering the effect of increasing solar radiation. The findings suggest that the energy flux may increase even further at shorter distances to the sun due to a lower rate of energy flux than previous models show, and the rate of this increase matches predictions made based on observations of the Earth's magnetosphere. The studies also revealed a daily cycle in energy flux that is highest in the early morning hours, and the patterns vary by orbital distance. The data indicate that the energy flux is influenced by solar wind particles flowing back towards the sun, known as the solar breeze, and the rate of this movement matches the speed of the solar wind. The research concluded that the energy flux and solar wind speed slow down at the same rate in the outer region of the inner heliosphere but that the energy flux increases more in the inner region due to the energy gained from the solar radiation and the solar breeze. The findings can be used to improve computer models of the inner heliosphere and the solar system as a whole and have implications for the study of space weather on other planets near the inner edge of our solar system. The data from the Parker Solar Probe mission demonstrate the importance of direct observations in understanding the complex interactions within the inner heliosphere. Thanks to speech-emotion-based applications such as human-computer interaction and biometric monitoring, detecting emotions in speech has become a widely sought-after topic in both academia and industry. Although deep learning-based models have significantly improved speech emotion recognition, their performance suffers when adapting to new domains. This issue is particularly challenging in speech emotion recognition, where conditions such as noise levels and temperature vary greatly from one domain to another. To address this challenge, we present a novel domain adaptation approach using deep reinforcement learning, which targets a key aspect of domain adaptation called intra-domain variability. We achieve this by training a single model that can distinguish between different data samples, without being aware of an artificially created label. This is done by teaching the model to prefer a subset of highly representative and diverse data samples, which facilitates efficient generalization to new domains. We validate our approach on speech emotion recognition data and observe a 14% improvement in average accuracy compared to conventional techniques. Moreover, our method excels in low-data-sample scenarios, delivering a 12% boost in average accuracy. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of our approach on a widely used biometric dataset, introducing a novel strategy to handle domain adaptation in a semi-supervised setting. This involves combining our deep reinforcement learning method with conventional techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation, which yields a 15% improvement in average accuracy on this particular dataset. Our code is available online at this link: https://github.com/ghrasoul/SpeechEmotionRecognition.

A persistent issue in signal processing from physical systems has been addressed by developing an objective method to treat non-stationarity in time series data. This approach enables structural analysis of time series, revealing the content of lower-frequency components that underlie apparent higher-frequency noise. We applied this method to investigate the sound produced by peeling an adhesive tape, a phenomenon known as crackling noise that resembles non-random movement. Our findings reveal a constant time interval between the occurrence of a peak in the power spectrum and a corresponding change in the signal's structure, suggesting that the noise is, in fact, random rather than non-random. Furthermore, we found that the distribution of time intervals between these peaks conforms to an exponential distribution, supporting the conclusion that the noise is stochastic in nature. Our results also show that the noise's entropy remains constant over time, indicating that the peeling process generates sound in a self-similar manner. Our study demonstrates the usefulness of signal processing from physical systems by providing a precise definition of random noise that underlies many physical systems and potentially misidentifying non-random noise. Our approach and the explicit parameters extracted from the tape-peeling system can serve as models for other systems that generate similar noise, allowing for a deeper understanding of phenomena like crackling noise in the brain during multiple sclerosis patients or sound produced by geological processes that precede earthquakes. Our study is also relevant to the broader context of entropy and self-similarity in time series data. Our approach provides a quantitative measure of randomness that can be applied to other systems and may have implications for fields like finance, geophysics, and medicine that frequently encounter and attempt to interpret complex time series data. Our method and the findings from the tape-peeling system can be applied to other systems that generate sound in a self-similar manner, offering a promising direction for future research. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with high sensitivity. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to missing or incorrectly measuring components of the spectrum due to instrumental limitations such as radio frequency interference, hardware malfunctions, systematic errors, and incomplete sky coverage. Consequently, developers are placing greater emphasis on simulating instrumental effects accurately in order to design efficient detection strategies and optimize data analysis for mountable data. Despite this, there's currently a lack of suitable tools for simulating instrumental effects on cosmic microwave background spectra. It also offers versatile simulations of cosmic microwave background signals and supports multi-core processing. Furthermore, the program facilitates easy exchange of parameters with other tools and provides transparent documentation of simulations. As such, s4cmb can be utilized as a standalone tool for researching cosmic microwave background spectra or in conjunction with other frameworks for more comprehensive analysis. In the task of arranging words into a meaningful sentence, both human and automated systems can typically determine the correct order. While both rely on a grammar rule system for guidance, the mechanistic basis behind this process is not well understood for automated methods, especially when using pre-trained language models. This study employs BART as a case study to better understand the mechanisms underlying word arrangement. Through the use of counterfactual language models and strategically constructed test cases, our analysis reveals that BAR's dependence on linguistic knowledge in this context is weak, and its ability to arrange words correctly is primarily a result of its ability to generate coherent sentences. Additionally, we find that training datasets play a significant role in the performance of these models, and that BART's strong performance is largely due to the presence of similar sentence-arrangement tasks in the WebText dataset it was trained on. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that evaluating the task with metrics based on reference sentences may lead to inaccurate results, and that more appropriate evaluation methods may involve the use of contextual knowledge similar to that used in other information retrieval tasks. We also present a method for simplifying the task evaluation by removing the need for reference sentences, and demonstrate that this method outperforms traditional evaluation methods based on reference sentences. We conclude by highlighting the scope for future work in this area, and stressing the importance of examining the underlying mechanisms of automated systems in the context of word arrangement. We have made the data and code associated with this study available online for the benefit of others.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable deepfake detection system for ensuring online content safety. Our research introduces a novel MD-CSDNetwork, a multi-domain cross stitched network that detects deepfakes by combining two parallel branches employing stitched filters to match low-frequency light fields and convert them into high-frequency images. By converting low-frequency light fields through two separate networks, we ensure that one image belongs to the real category and use them to determine the deepfake type, thereby enhancing detection accuracy. Our system surpasses the current state-of-the-art models by achieving the top results in both CIFADataset and FF++Dataset and we propose a straightforward method to extend it to multi-class deepfake detection, allowing it to simultaneously detect multiple types of deepfake images with outstanding performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/Chengzyh/MD-CSDNetwork.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the function's properties. Over time, researchers encountered these problems and attempted to solve them, yet ultimately were unable to do so. This article aims to provide a concise introduction to the noted problems and outline our successful resolution of them. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We have published the research in the form of a catalog featuring the basic properties of the 19 candidates assessed in this study. We have also included 19 additional previously documented bulge cluster candidates assessed in a similar manner for comparative purposes. The entire record now stands at 38 unverified globular cluster candidates within the galaxy's bulge. The research relied on data collected during the initial six years of the VVV survey and incorporated additional information from the OGLE, 2MASS, and Gaia databases. The overall assessment awaits verification through observational means but provides a comprehensive starting point for future research, also offering a comparative analysis with previously documented bulge cluster candidates. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotating or translating their input data. To address this vulnerability, our research introduces a novel concept called transformation uniqueness in the output of these models when input data varies in its geometric representation. We have found specific models' output values become unique once the orientation of a local geometric structure is established, even if the structure's position changes. Leveraging this unique property, we have developed an efficient and robust smoothing algorithm for point cloud models called Transformation-Unique Smoothing using Projection (TPS-P), which simplifies complex transformations like n-dimensional affine transformations. TPS-P primarily focuses on smoothing local geometric structures that possess unique orientations, thereby ensuring the output of point cloud models remains unaffected by position changes. We have also explored a more comprehensive version called TPS, which smooths over all possible transformations, and tested both versions extensively on publicly available datasets. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement in robustness and the ability to resist various environmental hazards like rain or fog, while point cloud models trained with TPS show a minor decrease in accuracy comparable to baseline models. Nonetheless, our innovative approach breaks new ground in tackling various real-world applications that involve point cloud models prone to manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabir/TPC.

This approach enables us to investigate the transmission of solutions by considering the connection between layers, rather than the specifics of the inter-layer connections. By leveraging this method, we are able to determine the conditions under which solutions can be transmitted across layers and the resulting dynamics on a multilayer network. Our study on a representative example demonstrates how our approach can be applied to complex multilayer networks, featuring both identical and heterogeneous component networks. In this study, the stress-strain relationship for an isotropic material is analyzed to demonstrate how the comprehensive Cauchy stress operator can be simplified to its most fundamental form, eliminating unnecessary parameterizations while upholding consistency with material response observations. A comprehensive examination of the stress operator's properties reveals that its most basic representation consists of a scalar function of the second invariant of the rate-of-deformation tensor, often overlooked in previous discussions. To illustrate the significance of this finding, a numerical approach is employed to determine the explicit parameters for a wide range of materials, including elastic, plastic, and damage models.
