For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having an effective mapping technique is crucial. In this research, we introduce HiTMap, a novel navigation map format featuring interconnected circular modules, and we demonstrate the efficacy of this representation in particular, consisting of triangular sub-modules within its circular components. We have conducted comprehensive simulations to evaluate the performance of HiTMap, mapping it against an ideal global mapping approach. Our findings, set against a backdrop of existing research, reveal that HiTMap outperforms current methods in various scenarios. Furthermore, we explore the practical applications of HiTMap in real-world settings, and we believe that this map format has significant potential for use with a variety of navigation algorithms. Our navigation maps are completely independent of location-based references, relying instead on absolute directions that define each map element. As a result, HiTMap provides a compact and flexible framework even when the surrounding environment is complex and extensive. We have made HiTMap available online for public access. Our research has been focused on the theoretical aspects of HiTMap, and we have numerous ideas for further development, including integrating HiTMap with existing filtering prediction algorithms and evaluating its performance in real-world settings through physical robot experiments. Our default implementation of HiTMap has been created using Python, and our map visualization tool can be run using the Python package PyQt5. Our research has also been conducted with the aim of addressing the uncertainty that arises when navigating in unfamiliar environments, and we have numerous approaches to further investigate this challenge, including developing methods to integrate HiTMap with filtering prediction algorithms, evaluating the efficacy of HiTMap in dynamic environments, and exploring methods to tackle the uncertainty that gives rise to holes in the navigation map. Our default implementation of HiTMap provides a basic map visualization tool, and our research has been focused on the navigation map representation rather than the detection methods themselves. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields, especially in areas near interacting magnetic moments, where atomic interferometry's effectiveness is compromised by the instability of interference patterns caused by permanent magnetic fields. This issue can be resolved by placing a material that exhibits the Meissner effect, expelling magnetic fields from its interior, in close proximity to atomic interferometry equipment. This simple trick enables the detection of extremely faint magnetic fields within atomic shells by analyzing expelled field patterns, and can even determine the source of the field's gradient to enhance spatial field resolution. This novel atomic interferometry approach has significant applications in evaluating and controlling quantum systems, as well as in conducting precise measurements of interaction forces between matter and light. Moreover, by leveraging the finite dimensions of materials that demonstrate the Meissner effect, researchers can now accurately measure local field variations and the response of atomic shells to these variations, thereby gaining valuable insights into interference pattern stability and expanding the capabilities of atomic interferometry to include cultural applications, such as monitoring field variations in laboratory settings. Lastly, this discovery demonstrates that atomic interferometry can be used to derive theoretical aspects of the Meissner effect in over simple scenarios, consisting of interacting degrees of freedom, mean-field effects, and non-equilibrium conditions.

This study investigates finite mixture models through the lens of stochastic convex geometry. We demonstrate that mixing models with convex weights correspond to the superposition of geometric objects defined by the model's components, which can be characterized using support functions. This formulation enables the calculation of a model's performance measures, such as its mean and variance, as the weighted sum of its components' performance measures. Furthermore, we find that regression models based on mixing distributions can be expressed as the sum of the models based on the individual components, allowing us to draw inferences about the mixing distribution from these models. We also explore the relationship between mixing models and their identifiability issue, as well as the generation of realistic data sets using these models. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework for evaluating the diversity of populations or datasets, which can be applied to problems such as overfitting. This study is an invitation to researchers from machine learning to explore stochastic convex geometry and its applications, which can be theoretically and practically illustrated with simple simulations. Moreover, we demonstrate how this framework can be applied to real-world problems, such as the analysis of cells' morphology. Lastly, we discuss some open research questions in this domain.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices like GPUs requires object-based programming, which can be challenging due to limited register resources and inefficient memory usage. Despite the efficiency of stack-based memory allocation, it hasn't been widely used on GPUs because existing implementations fail to utilize full parallelism and struggle with small thread blocks. In response, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel stack allocator designed to excel in object-based GPU programming. By introducing a new binary allocation tree data structure and multiple scanning threads, DynaSOAr achieves significant improvements in performance, memory utilization, and speed, outperforming leading cache and heap allocators in various applications. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's compact size enables efficient storage on GPUs, and its flexible design allows for seamless integration with existing compilers and tools. We have tested DynaSOAr extensively, demonstrating its capabilities across a range of benchmarks, including popular deep learning frameworks, and providing detailed analysis of performance gains and memory usage. The DynaSOAr allocator is currently available for use with the NVIDIA CUDA programming model. In addition to the allocator, we have created a simple stack-based programming model, which includes example code and guidelines for writing stack-based GPU applications. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from $500$ to $700$ million years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. Although direct imaging is challenging, TOI-712 is suitable for study through spectroscopic analysis, and the team found it has an orbital inclination of $89.82$ degrees, a surface gravity of $4.6$ degrees, and an inclination of $1.8$ degrees among its stellar characteristics. Despite finding no signs of planetary activity, the team discovered weak stellar oscillations and a metallicity of $0.16$ or $14\%$. Ultimately, TOI-712 offers promising prospects for future exoplanet characterization and direct imaging, as well as potential study of stellar evolution and planetary migration. The team also found a likely astrophysical noise component with a $12.48$ day period associated with the star's rotation, which is similar to the discovery of a $12.4$ day period in the K2 data. The team further analyzed this system using the K2 mission, with a new exoplanet detection called TOI-712 d, and also found evidence of external flickers, as well as a dust emission around a nearby star called 2MASS J06435742 $+264� 3577$. We investigated the electronic and magnetic structure of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO$_{2}$ using periodic density functional theory. As the concentration varies, from point defects to bulk doped TiO$_{2}$, we examined the theoretical models, including effective single-body Hamiltonians and GGA+U methods. The results show that substitutional carbon and nitrogen possess an s^2 configuration and an open shell configuration respectively, whereas the N dimers exhibit both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic properties. Additionally, we found that nitrogen defects have a significant effect on the surrounding oxygen atoms, potentially leading to localized states and allowing for self-doping behavior. Moreover, the study highlights the difficulty of describing N defects using the effective single-body Hamiltonian approach. Moreover, we explored the experimental spectroscopic data and validated our results by analyzing the K edge X-ray absorption spectra of Ti and O atoms in the TiO$_{2}$ matrices doped with C and N. Lastly, we investigated the effects of dopant concentration and lattice parameter on the electronic and magnetic properties, and discussed possible mechanisms of self-doping and magnetism driven by strain and electron-phonon interactions. Lastly, we examined the phases of Ti, O, N atoms at high temperature and pressure, and recovered the experimental and theoretical results of phase transitions in TiN$_{x}$O$_{y}$ compounds.

This letter proposes a strategy for detecting top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider through elastic proton-proton scattering. By searching for a clear signature of high-transverse-energy photons or jets accompanied by missing transverse energy, our approach identifies a characteristic pattern of scattered protons in the forward detectors of the LHC. Utilizing a dedicated technique to reconstruct highly displaced protons, our method leverages the full potential of the LHC's energy and includes an innovative strategy to make effective use of the CERN Detector complex's extensive coverage. Initial tests using data from the Run 2 at the LHC reveal the potential for detecting elastic top-quark pairs with data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments, with expected cross-section sensitivity of roughly 0.01 fb. Furthermore, as the energy of the LHC continues to increase during Run 3 and Run 4, our method predicts a detectable cross-section of 1 fb for elastic top-quark production with subsequent studies of elastic production for various processes, including the rare decay of Higgs bosons and additional sources of energy that may be hidden. The proposed analysis for elastic top-quark production facilitates effective use of the LHC's full capability, exploits the uniqueness of elastic scattering to efficiently suppress inelastic background, and provides a versatile method that can be applied to a range of rare processes involving forward jets and missing transverse energy. The design of the proposed temperature detector includes a switchable buffer option, enabling both inverting and sourcing modes of operation. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, a phenomenon supported by various theories, including the concept that cores require a minimum amount of mass to initiate outflows and form high-mass stars.  By comparing the mass distributions of cores and the mass functions of the most massive stars formed within the cloud, researchers found that the mass function of the cores exceeds the mass function of the formed stars, with the exception of the most massive cores (top 10%).  These exceptional cores, with masses greater than 25 solar masses, are capable of giving birth to the most massive stars formed within the cloud, including O-stars.  This study further finds that the average mass of the cores that remain starless for a short period of time is significantly greater than the average mass of the cores that remain starless for a long period of time.  This finding is consistent with the idea that only cores with masses greater than a certain threshold can initiate outflows and form high-mass stars, although it can also be explained by other mechanisms, such as the destruction of dense cores by external radiation.  The evidence presented here for the role of core mass in initiating outflows and forming high-mass stars is novel, whereas the common occurrence of massive stars forming within dark cloud cores that give birth to molecular outflows is now well documented.  The relationship between core mass and the formation of high-mass stars provides a critical ingredient for the development of theoretical models that simulate the formation of high-mass stars, including O-stars, and has important implications for the origin of massive star clusters and the regulation of the formation of stars in the galaxy. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by a rough surface's texture, which can be hazardous for safety in various contexts such as waterways, surface skidding, and gas well screening. Despite the importance of this issue, there's a lack of understanding about how surface textures interact with specific types of liquids, prompting the need for this study. We've specifically examined the interaction between a rough surface and liquid foams, which exhibit unique and challenging characteristics during experimentation due to their fragile and deformable nature. To overcome this difficulty, we designed a precise apparatus that allows for controlled movement and accurate measurement of the forces acting between a diamond-knife surface and glycerol-based liquid foams in various bubble sizes. Our detailed analysis of these interactions has revealed that the formation of sharp edges and points within the surface texture can lead to surprisingly high static friction forces, often exceeding the weight that they support by several times. This surprising finding challenges the long-held assumption that static friction is generally equal to the supported weight. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the surface texture's effect on friction can be significant, with a found increase of up to 100% in static friction forces when the surface knighthood is altered from sharp to rounded edges. Our research has been carried out using a specific surface knighthood and glycerol-based liquid foams, but our results are expected to be applicable to a broader range of surfaces and liquids, including water, oil, and chemical substances. Our novel discovery of texture-induced friction in liquid foams provides important insights for safety in various contexts and could also lead to innovative technologies such as improved well screens and specialized surface treatments. Lastly, our results for liquid foams offer a solution to the long-standing issue of measuring static friction forces, which has significant implications for the theoretical understanding of flow and friction in complex liquids. This research investigates the long-term behavior of a specific type of random walk, denoted as $M^n_t$, which is derived from a simple symmetric random walk, $X^n_t$, using the formula $M^n_t = \frac{1}{2} \left( \sqrt{\lambda^n_t} \cdot \text{sign}(X^n_t) \right)^2$, where the function $\lambda^n_t$ represents the local time of the random walk $X^n_t$ at time $t$. Our main conclusion is that the probability $P\left( M^n_t > \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+t/n}} - \sqrt{2\log(1+t/n)} \right)^2 \right)$ eventually converges to one as $t$ approaches infinity. Additionally, a more specific result shows that the probability $P\left( M^n_t > \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+t/n}} - \epsilon \right)^2 \right)$ also converges to zero as $t$ approaches infinity for any positive value of $\epsilon$. It's worth noting that these findings expand upon existing results in the field of random walk local time behavior. Existing research has examined both the upper and lower bounds of $M^n_t$ and found that both converge to a specific value as $t$ approaches infinity. On the other hand, the current research focuses on the probability that $M^n_t$ exceeds a particular value as $t$ approaches infinity and provides a new approach to analyzing this behavior. The approach used in this research involves applying the Chernoff bound in conjunction with upper bounds on $M^n_t$ in order to achieve the desired outcome. The current research also offers the opportunity to comment on a prior result related to $X^n_t$ rather than $M^n_t$. The prior result established that the probability that $X^n_t$ exceeds a particular value as $t$ approaches infinity is determined by the ratio of $t$ to the base two power of $n$ and concluded that this ratio converges to a specific value as $t$ approaches infinity. In contrast, the current research finds that the probability that $M^n_t$ exceeds a particular value as $t$ approaches infinity is driven by the ratio of the base two power of $t$ to the base two power of $n$ and determined that this ratio also converges to a specific value as $t$ approaches infinity. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. This paper focuses on analyzing plasma properties and confirming the helicon mode of discharge in the IShTAR plasma source. A mathematical model was used to predict the occurrence of the helicon mode, and factors that influence it, such as power and magnetic field strength. However, this model overestimated the required magnetic field strength, and an alternative explanation based on the facility's design was proposed. Furthermore, a study was conducted to identify the helicon mode's characteristic sound emissions, and a relationship between the mode and plasma density was established. Additionally, a transition occurred from the helicon mode to the electro magnetic mode when the plasma density became too high, and this transition was found to be influenced by both the rate of plasma density change and the magnitude of plasma density. This knowledge is crucial for optimizing the plasma source to maintain the helicon mode of discharge, and it has been demonstrated how this can be achieved by adjusting various parameters, such as the rate of plasma density change, the magnitude of plasma density, the strength of the magnetic field, and the level of radio frequency power. This has the benefit of improving plasma density while preventing the helicon mode from switching to the electromagnetic mode, and it has been shown that this can be accomplished in the IShTAR plasma source. This paper complements an earlier report that focused on the experimental investigation of the IShTAR device, and it provides a more in depth analysis of the results. This more in depth analysis has been presented in the form of six additional figures that illustrate various aspects of the results, and these figures along with the existing four figures that were presented in the earlier report, are now available in the appendix. This more in depth analysis has also been previously discussed in detail at ICRF conference in 2018, and in the context of the European Fusion Edge Program. This paper is intended for an audience that is familiar with the IShTAR test facility, and it provides a direct access to the results, figures, and the appendix. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively evaluating nucleus segmentation solutions is challenging due to the absence of suitable golden standards. In this paper, a novel W-Net architecture is presented, capable of pinpointing and highlighting nucleus centers within biological samples. Emphasizing ease of implementation, the network comprises just 19 Convolutional Neural Network parameters, and we advocate for its use as a pre-training block by the scientific community. Furthermore, as there are no established metrics for evaluating nucleus segmentation, a novel Measure of Spatial Scatter (MOSS) score is proposed to assess the quality of nucleus segmentations. The functionality of the MOSS score was demonstrated across various biological imaging scenarios, and it was found to be sensitive to the presence of gold standard standards, rendering it suitable for use in evaluation protocols. Deep Neural Network techniques, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained remarkable precision in tackling complex graph-level classifications and predictions. However, the underlying mathematical principles of these networks, particularly the connection to the theory of linear filtering and optimization, remain unexplored in the scientific community. In order to bridge this knowledge gap, we provide a non-technical explanation of GCNNs from a biological perspective, leveraging analogies with the natural world. We demonstrate that the operation of GCNNs shares common ground with the concept of matched filtering, which is a fundamental idea in signal processing that forms the basis of linear filtering and optimization. A simple GCNN model, which we call a "Simple Spectral GCNN" (SS-GCNN), is derived from this framework by utilizing signal processing principles to analyze spectral data. We further investigate the relationship between traditional GCNNs and SS-GCNN, revealing that both result in identical outcomes when the number of network layers exceeds a certain threshold. We evaluate the performance of both networks on a set of real-world datasets, which includes chemical compound activity prediction, social network influence prediction, and genetic mutation classification, among others. Our results show that both the simple and standard GCNN models exhibit comparable performance in these experiments. We believe that this paper provides a novel insight into the mathematical foundations of GCNNs, offers a biological interpretation of this network, and presents a new, efficiently trained GCNN model capable of handling spectral data. We anticipate that this work will serve as a starting point for further exploration of the underlying principles of GCNNs, along with its biological and signal processing implications. We have publicly available code for the SS-GCNN model, which can be found at https://github.com/yousef-ali/shallow-spectral-GCNN. We further discuss potential future work, including the analysis of deeper networks, the development of a theoretical connection between network depth and smoothness, and the investigation of localized GCNNs. We propose the research question of proving that both the standard and simple networks result in identical outcomes when the number of network layers exceeds three, as the central challenge of this paper. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our aim is to demonstrate that there is an inherent relationship between algorithms and proofs, which can be represented through the lens of logical pseudocodes. Furthermore, this framework provides a means for deriving executions plans from the perspective of forward reasoning, as well as offering a solution to the problem of deciding whether a given statement is safe or not. Additionally, we offer a discussion on the relationship between logical pseudocodes and natural deduction, as well as a brief examination of the related concept of web correctness. Moreover, we introduce a new form of cut operation, which can be used to extend the natural deduction system, which is based on the Godel natural deduction system. This new form of cut operation is both sound and complete, and it possesses the property of preserving persistence. Lastly, we conclude by discussing the potential applications of logical pseudocodes in various settings, ranging from the examination of imperative algorithms with the sequent calculus, to the generation of execution plans, as well as in the context of static safety checking. In the context of data analysis, a variation of the $k$-centers problem is often utilized to create a simplified representation of complex data sets. This problem involves identifying the minimum number of points needed to represent a given dataset, such that each point in the dataset is associated with the nearest center. This task can be seen as a mapping between the original data and a more concise representation, effectively defining a clustering of the data. The problem has been extensively studied for static data sets across various metrics, however, the focus shifts to the implementation of the algorithm on dynamic data sets, where frequent additions and deletions of data points occur. In this study, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently handling the update of dynamic data sets for the $k$-centers problem, with an optimal time complexity of $O(k^2 \Delta^2)$ for each update, where $\Delta$ represents the dimension of the data set. This achievement is made possible by the introduction of a new geometric concept called the shadow center, which enables the application of existing results from the static problem to the dynamic problem. Furthermore, we demonstrate the algorithm's performance across various real-world and synthetic data sets, with results showing its superior performance in comparison to existing algorithms. Finally, we outline a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's efficacy, with an analysis of the algorithm's time complexity and a comparison with the best available static algorithm, thereby highlighting the trade-offs between the efficacy of the static and dynamic algorithms. From a practical perspective, we show that the algorithm can be optimized for lower time complexity for certain data sets, with an example provided in the paper. Lastly, we conclude the study by outlining potential applications and future enhancements of the algorithm. We introduce a novel type of stochastic chase-evasion games on directed graph models, extending existing work by incorporating hierarchical representations and separating regions into evader-safe and attacker-penetrable areas. Unlike standard dynamic game formulations, the evaluation of a node in these graphs considers the complex interaction of various regions, rather than a unified win/lose outcome. We develop two distinct hierarchical decompositions of these stochastic chase-evasion games, focusing on optimized policy implementation and compact representation. These hierarchical methods can be combined to tackle large-scale problems, and we show that our approach can be set within the framework of hierarchical reinforcement learning, leveraging the efficiency of smaller-subproblem solutions to expedite the completion of large-scale stochastic chase-evasion tasks. We validate our proposed models through extensive simulations conducted on synthetic graphs, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach and identifying areas for future improvement. benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task

performance and lead to catastrophic forgetting of initial tasks as new ones are
introduced. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through an innovative pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural network. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation by utilizing a deeply cascaded autoregressive architecture, yet its limited pitch control results from converted learned features instead of direct pitch influence. To overcome this constraint, we introduce a pitch-dependent expanded convolutional network where each stage consists of multiple convolutional layers with different filter banks, whose inputs are combined using vector-based attention. The proposed model excels at generating speech with diverse pitch characteristics while maintaining comparable quality to WN-based models, as proven by comprehensive experiments conducted on the LJSpeech dataset. Moreover, QPNet demonstrates superior style transfer speech synthesis on the VCTK dataset, yielding a significant 10.48 MOS scores when compared to WN-based models. We utilize a dataset that combines styled and genuine X-ray images along with corresponding medical diagnoses, and evaluate our proposal through a new task called neural styling refinement, where the goal is to reverse the changes made by these photo editing models to retrieve genuine X-ray images. In a notable achievement, our research sets a new record among neural networking achievements by showcasing that a complex architecture can successfully achieve outstanding results in refining edited X-ray images, even when given limited information about the underlying condition. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and in-depth examination, designed to accommodate user-created scripts for custom operations and calculations. The tool, tailored for user interaction, enables efficient exploration of large datasets by performing operations such as component separation, conversion between data formats, and advanced statistical analyses, as well as creating interactive 3D visualizations. ViDaExpert supports multiple programming languages, including R, MATLAB, and Python, and can be modified to suit specific research needs. The application and documentation are available freely. The name ViDaExpert is short for Vectorial Data Expert, reflecting the tool's capabilities in vectorial data analysis and comprehensive problem-solving. The development of ViDaExpert was funded by the German Research Foundation, specifically the DFG Research Training Group "Methods and Models for Natural Convection", and the application is licensed under the GPL v2. The application and additional information can be found online at www.vidaexpert.de. The name ViDaExpert is also an acronym for Visualization and Data Expert.
